Run npx @redocly/cli lint openapi.yaml or npx @stoplight/spectral-cli lint openapi.yaml. | Check your mocks against it. npx @stoplight/prism-cli mock openapi.yaml serves a mock API from the document, so you can build a client before you have credentials. | Run the reference implementation locally. The repository’s devserver serves every route at http://localhost:8080 with no AWS account. See the repository’s README → Local development. The Interactive Reference can send requests to it once its origin is allowed. See the steps at the top of the Interactive Reference. | .

247.title: Versioning and change policy
247.content: The API version is the Substratal-Version request header (currently 1), not part of the base URL. Every versioned operation declares it as the shared ApiVersion header parameter (components.parameters.ApiVersion), so generated clients include it, and the Interactive Reference sends it for you. Most generators let you set it once as a default header instead of passing it per call. info.version in the document (currently a 1.0.0-draft pre-release) is the version of the document itself. | Additive changes (new optional fields, new operations, new enum values) ship within the current version. Write clients to ignore fields they don’t know, and to handle enum values they don’t recognize. | Breaking changes ship as the next version number, and the previous version keeps working for at least 6 months. See Non-Functional Requirements → Versioning for what counts as breaking. | Every change is recorded in the Changelog. | .

248.title: Substratal Apps — Platform API
248.content: When your business is building applications, Substratal Apps removes the user-management burden: one API for user accounts, settings, organizations/tenancy, and per-user storage, so a developer can focus entirely on the app they’re actually trying to build. This site specifies that API: who a user is, what they’re allowed to touch within a given app, and how each app’s own settings and data are stored and scoped. It is API-first — no end-user interface is specified here. A dashboard that makes onboarding easier is planned, but it’s a client of this API, built later, not a requirement to use it today.

249.title: What Substratal Apps actually is
249.content: Think of it as the user/organization/tenancy layer that an app developer would otherwise have to build themselves — comparable in shape to Auth0, Clerk, or WorkOS, but scoped around the full set of things a multi-tenant app needs from day one, not just login: accounts, per-app and per-org settings, team/tenancy structure, and a place to store the app’s own per-user data, all behind one API. An Application in this spec is one developer’s app, built on top of Substratal Apps for that layer. Today, every Application is built by Substratal itself; a marketplace where outside developers register and manage their own Applications is an explicit later phase — see App developer/publisher model. The Entitlement that gates a user’s access to an app, and the billing relationship behind it, belongs to that app’s own developer. For Substratal’s own catalog that’s Substratal, through the Free/Standard subscription on Pricing; a future third-party developer bills their own users outside this API. See Billing system of record.

250.title: What this site is
250.content: This is a living specification and the system of record for the platform API. It isn’t a one-time design doc — as decisions get made and the API gets built, this site is where that gets reflected. If this site and a conversation, a Slack thread, or an old draft disagree, this site wins; update it the moment something here goes stale. It’s written to be read by people building the API and by AI coding tools asked to work against it — see /llms.txt for a machine-oriented index of every page.

251.title: How it’s organized
251.content: | Section | Answers | . | Getting Started | Where to start if you’re new to this — human or AI tool. | . | Quickstart | A runnable curl walkthrough — create a user, grant an app, check access, turn it off. | . | Domain Model | What are the core entities, and how do they relate? | . | Access Control | Given a user and an app, what decides if a request is allowed? | . | API Reference | What are the actual resources, endpoints, and payloads? Includes Auth (signup, login, app tokens), Push Notifications (alerts and updates to a User’s devices, and their inbox), and Billing (the Free/Standard subscription). The OpenAPI Specification section renders the whole contract as interactive Swagger UI. | . | OpenAPI Specification | The full contract as OpenAPI 3.1: interactive Swagger UI, download, client generation, and how to read it. | . | Workflows | How do the pieces move together for real scenarios — a purchase, an admin revoking access, a role change? | . | Trust Model | How does a separately-hosted app verify a user’s access without maintaining its own user table? | . | MCP Server | How does an AI agent call this API directly, as a tool-using client rather than writing HTTP calls by hand? | . | Non-Functional Requirements | Security, multi-tenancy, audit, rate limits, versioning. | . | Compliance & Data Protection | Which of SOC 2, HIPAA, GDPR, and CCPA apply, and when to act on each. | . | Legal | Terms of Service, Privacy Policy, EULA, Developer Terms, the Data Processing Addendum, and the other agreements, at stable URLs. | . | Roadmap | What ships in the MVP vs. later phases. | . | Pricing | Free and Standard ($6 per user per month) — what people using Substratal’s apps pay, individually or through an Organization. | . | Changelog | What’s changed in this spec over time. | . | Glossary | Precise definitions for every term used here. | .

252.title: The one idea worth remembering
252.content: Two questions get asked, separately, every time a user touches an app: . | Is the app itself switched on for this user? This is the Entitlement — a literal on/off record, independent of what the user could do if it were on. An admin flipping a user’s access to an app off is a write to this record, nothing else. | If it’s on, what can they do? This is the Role — platform-wide or scoped to that one app — resolved into a set of Permissions. | . Everything else in this spec (profiles, settings, orders, audit) hangs off of that split. See Access Control for the full model. This site is self-hosting its own context: it’s generated from Markdown committed to this same repository, under docs/, via GitHub Pages. It’s deliberately scoped to the API specification itself: how a developer or their AI agent builds against this API. How it’s deployed is in the repository’s infra/README.md, and what’s left to build is in plan-remaining.md; the repo’s README.md maps what’s where.

254.title: MCP Server
254.content: A Model Context Protocol server that lets an AI agent or chat client operate the Platform API directly — list a user’s entitlements, toggle one off, request a Tenant tier change — without the calling agent (or the person prompting it) hand-rolling REST calls. | Why this exists | What this is not | Transport & endpoint | Authentication — no new model | Tool surface is generated, not hand-authored | Tool annotations & safety . | Destructive operations | . | Statelessness | Resources | Where this runs | .

255.title: Why this exists
255.content: Everything in the API Reference is already callable by any HTTP client. What an LLM-driven client specifically needs on top of that is a tool-call interface — a typed, discoverable list of operations it can invoke, with structured results it can reason over — rather than a human having to describe curl commands to it. MCP is the emerging standard shape for that interface; this server is Substratal’s own implementation of it, aimed at the same audience as everything else in this spec: a support engineer’s AI assistant, an internal ops agent, a customer’s own agent calling me-scoped endpoints on their own behalf. This is a new surface, not a new capability. Every tool call ultimately executes the exact same Access Control algorithm, the exact same permission checks, the exact same Audit Event trail as the equivalent REST call — see Authentication below. Building this is translation work, not new business logic.

256.title: What this is not
256.content: . | Not a new Application. It doesn’t appear in the Application catalog, doesn’t hold an Entitlement, and isn’t owned by a Tenant. It’s a protocol gateway in front of the same API every other caller uses — closer in kind to the hub dashboard than to a downstream app. | Not a new trust relationship. Trust Model describes how a separately-hosted Application verifies a user’s access; that’s unrelated to this page, which describes how an agent calls this hub’s own API. The two are complementary, not overlapping. | Not a replacement for the REST API or openapi.yaml. It’s a generated view over the same contract — see Tool surface is generated, not hand-authored. | .

257.title: Transport & endpoint
257.content: POST https://api.substratalapps.com/mcp . Implements MCP’s Streamable HTTP transport: a single endpoint, JSON-RPC 2.0 request/response bodies, with the client’s Mcp-Session-Id header (issued on initialize) tying together the calls in one session. Deliberately on the existing api.substratalapps.com domain rather than a new mcp. subdomain — no new Route 53 zone or ACM certificate needed, consistent with Deployment Architecture → Cost principles. Deliberately not versioned by Substratal-Version — this endpoint isn’t a REST resource, and MCP has its own protocol-version negotiation (a date-based version string exchanged during initialize) that’s independent of this API’s own version header. The MCP server makes every tool call with the API version its tools describe, so an MCP client never sends the header — the same “versioned independently” pattern Non-Functional Requirements → Versioning already applies to webhook payloads. Tier 0’s implementation is deliberately the simplest conforming option: every tool call returns one buffered JSON response, no server-initiated push, no mid-call progress notifications. See Deployment Architecture → MCP server for why that’s also the cheapest option, and what upgrading past it looks like.

258.title: Authentication — no new model
258.content: The MCP endpoint takes the exact same Authorization: Bearer <token> header as every other endpoint in Conventions — a user access token, or a scoped API Key. There is no MCP-specific credential, no separate consent/OAuth flow layered on top, and no elevated standing: the server holds no privilege of its own and simply forwards the caller’s own credential to the underlying REST call it’s translating a tool invocation into. A tool call a caller’s credential isn’t permitted to make fails exactly the way the equivalent curl call would — same 403, same error code. Because of this, the effective blast radius of connecting an agent to this server is entirely a function of which credential you hand it. Use an API Key created with intended_use: "agent": it defaults to restrict_destructive: true, which blocks destructive operations server-side regardless of the key’s permissions. An LLM deciding which tool to call is a different risk shape than deterministic service code doing the same thing. See API Keys → Agent keys & restrict_destructive.

259.title: Tool surface is generated, not hand-authored
259.content: Every MCP tool is generated from one operation in openapi.yaml — its operationId becomes the tool name (dots replaced with underscores, substratal_ prefixed), its parameters/request body become the tool’s input schema, and its summary/description become the tool’s description. This is a deliberate choice, not a shortcut: this spec already maintains openapi.yaml as the single machine-readable source of truth (see Conventions → Machine-readable); a hand-authored, separately-maintained MCP tool list would be a third copy of the API surface to keep in sync, on top of the prose and the YAML. Generating it means adding an endpoint to openapi.yaml is the only step required to also add it as a tool — nothing here needs separate maintenance. | operationId | MCP tool name | REST equivalent | . | entitlements.listForUser | substratal_entitlements_listForUser | GET /users/{id}/entitlements | . | entitlements.update | substratal_entitlements_update | PATCH /entitlements/{id} | . | permissions.getEffective | substratal_permissions_getEffective | GET /users/{id}/apps/{appId}/effective-permissions | . | tenants.requestTierChange | substratal_tenants_requestTierChange | POST /tenants/{id}/tier-change-requests | . | audit.list | substratal_audit_list | GET /audit-events | . (Illustrative, not exhaustive — every operation in openapi.yaml generates a tool this way, and that count grows as the spec grows. Deliberately not stated as a number here — any specific count written on this page would be wrong again the next time an endpoint is added, which is exactly the kind of drift this generation scheme exists to avoid. See openapi.yaml for the current, exact set; this page doesn’t duplicate that list.) . Build prerequisite: every operation in openapi.yaml now carries an operationId (added alongside this page specifically so this generation scheme is actually buildable, not aspirational) — see the Changelog entry for this addition. Adding a new endpoint going forward means adding its operationId at the same time, following the <resourceGroup>.<action> convention already in use (entitlements.update, tenants.requestTierChange), or it won’t get picked up by the generator.

260.title: Tool annotations & safety
260.content: MCP’s tool-definition schema supports annotations — readOnlyHint, destructiveHint, idempotentHint — that a compliant client (e.g. a chat app with a confirmation dialog) can use to decide whether to run a tool immediately or ask the user first. These are derived mechanically too, from information already in this spec rather than re-judged per tool: . | Annotation | Derived from | . | readOnlyHint: true | The operation is a GET. | . | destructiveHint: true | The operation carries x-substratal-destructive in openapi.yaml. That’s either always or conditional (destructive only for certain request bodies; the hint is still true, since a client can’t know in advance). The complete list is in Destructive operations below. | . | idempotentHint: true | The operation is a GET, PATCH, or DELETE (all idempotent in this API), or a POST that requires an Idempotency-Key. For those, the MCP server derives the key from a hash of the tool-call arguments, so a retried tool call can’t double-apply. | . Destructive operations . This table is the single source of truth. openapi.yaml’s x-substratal-destructive extension mirrors it operation by operation, and the server-side restrict_destructive check reads the same classification. | Operation | When destructive | . | Every DELETE | Always. That covers: user soft-delete, Entitlement delete-in-error, Role delete, Role-assignment removal, Organization member removal, webhook unsubscribe, API Key revoke, session revoke, MFA support-reset, erasure cancellation, push-device unregister, and push-credential removal. | . | PATCH /entitlements/{id} | When status becomes disabled or revoked. | . | PATCH /users/{id} | When status becomes suspended. | . | POST /users/{id}/suspend | Always. | . | POST /users/{id}/erasure-requests | Always. | . | PATCH /organizations/{id} | When status becomes suspended. | . | PATCH /organizations/{id}/members/{userId} | When it demotes an org_admin. | . | PATCH /applications/{id} | When review_status becomes rejected or suspended, or when available_app_roles/permissions shrink. | . | PATCH /roles/{id} | When permissions shrink. | . | POST /api-keys/{id}/rotate | Always. It breaks the current secret with no overlap. | . | PATCH /api-keys/{id} | When restrict_destructive is set to false. | . | POST /tenants/{id}/tier-change-requests and its PATCH | Always. They lead to a maintenance window. | . | POST /auth/logout with all_sessions: true | Always. | . | POST /users/{id}/sessions/revoke-all | Always. | . The same classification now has a second, server-side consumer, not just this client-facing hint: per API Keys → Agent keys & restrict_destructive, an API Key with restrict_destructive: true — the default for intended_use: "agent" keys — gets a hard 403 on exactly the operations this table classifies as destructive, regardless of what permissions the key otherwise carries. One classification, two effects: a well-behaved MCP client uses destructiveHint to decide whether to ask a human first; the platform uses the identical rule to decide whether to allow the call at all, for keys explicitly scoped that way.

261.title: Statelessness
261.content: An MCP session’s state (negotiated protocol version, declared client capabilities) is kept entirely in the Mcp-Session-Id the server hands back on initialize — a short-lived, signed, self-contained token, not a database row. Tier 0 needs no new table and no new database for this: every individual tool call is a single stateless Lambda invocation that decodes the session token, forwards the caller’s own Bearer credential to the matching REST call, and returns the result. See Deployment Architecture → MCP server for when (and why) this stops being enough.

262.title: Resources
262.content: Alongside tools, the server exposes a small, fixed set of MCP Resources — read-only context a client can fetch without it being a tool call — for an agent to ground itself before making tool calls: /llms.txt (the page index) and Glossary. Deliberately minimal; the tool surface is where the actual leverage is, and most of the rest of this site is already written to be read directly by an AI coding tool per Getting Started → If you’re an AI coding tool.

263.title: Where this runs
263.content: Build-out and AWS deployment — Tier 0 cost, and what triggers an upgrade — is specified alongside the rest of the platform’s infrastructure, not duplicated here: see Deployment Architecture → MCP server.

264.title: Non-Functional Requirements
264.content: . | Authentication | CORS | Authorization enforcement point | Multi-tenancy | Concurrency control | Transaction boundaries | Audit | Idempotency & retries | Rate limiting | Security logging | Service-level objectives | Versioning | Request tracing | Testing strategy | Data retention . | Audit log lifecycle | Hard-delete cascade | . | Availability expectations on the trust model | .

265.title: Authentication
265.content: . | User-facing login: native email/password, owned in-house, plus per-Organization SSO architected and deferred. See Auth → Native auth and per-Organization SSO. Tokens are RS256 JWTs signed with keys in AWS KMS and published at /.well-known/jwks.json. Platform access tokens live 15 minutes, app tokens 5 minutes, and refresh tokens are rotating and single-use with reuse detection. | Passwords: Argon2id (m=19456 KiB, t=2, p=1), 12–128 characters, checked against a bundled list of the 100,000 most common breached passwords. No composition rules, no forced rotation (NIST SP 800-63B). There’s no password column on users; credentials live on UserIdentity. | Brute-force protection: per-account lockout (5 failures in 15 minutes locks the account for 15 minutes), plus per-IP limits on every unauthenticated auth endpoint (see Rate limiting). Login errors never reveal whether an account exists. | MFA: optional TOTP (RFC 6238) for password identities, with 10 single-use recovery codes. TOTP secrets are encrypted with KMS at rest. An SSO identity’s MFA belongs to its IdP. | Service-to-service: billing → hub, app → hub, and any other backend caller authenticates with a scoped API Key, never user credentials. mTLS isn’t offered. | Secrets at rest: every bearer credential (refresh tokens, API Key secrets, emailed tokens, recovery codes) is stored only as a hash. Webhook signing secrets, TOTP secrets, and push credentials must be usable by the server, so they’re KMS-encrypted instead. So are push device tokens: they aren’t credentials, but they’re personal data the server has to send to. | Bootstrapping: the very first superadmin cannot be created through the public API — nothing can call POST /users/{id}/roles/{roleId} with roles.manage before a superadmin exists to grant it. It’s seeded directly against the database, not specified as an endpoint. Every deploy makes sure the platform owner’s account (the SUPERADMIN_EMAIL deploy variable) exists as a protected superadmin: active, verified, holding superadmin, and impossible to suspend, delete, erase, re-address, or demote, through the API (409 user_protected) or directly in the database. Its password is set with the one-time admin CLI (cmd/admin bootstrap) or the password-reset flow. | MCP: the MCP Server is not a separate auth surface — it carries and forwards the same Bearer credential (user token or API Key) as any other caller. No new rule in this section applies to it that doesn’t already apply here. | .

266.title: CORS
266.content: First-party web apps, such as the dashboard and an admin console, call this API straight from the browser with the signed-in person’s own User token. That’s safe without a backend in between: a Bearer token is never sent automatically the way a cookie is, so cross-site request forgery doesn’t apply, and the permission check on every request is the real gate. An admin console therefore sees exactly what its user’s Roles allow, no more. | Allow-listed origins may call any REST endpoint, with any method, sending Authorization, Content-Type, If-Match, Idempotency-Key, X-Request-Id, and Substratal-Version. Preflights are cached for 2 hours (Access-Control-Max-Age: 7200, the most Chromium honors), since an admin screen touches many /users/{id}/… URLs. | Readable response headers: ETag, X-Request-Id, RateLimit-Limit, RateLimit-Remaining, RateLimit-Reset, Retry-After, Audit-Hot-Window-Start, Substratal-Version, and, on a deprecated version, Deprecation and Sunset, so a web client can show that it needs updating. | Any other origin gets no CORS headers, so the browser blocks the response. | API Keys are never used from a browser. A key in a web page is a leaked key. A request that authenticates with an API Key and carries an Origin header, which browsers send and server-side clients don’t, is refused with 400 api_key_in_browser, whatever the origin. | . The exact allow-listed origins are an environment-level config value (CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS), not part of this spec.

267.title: Authorization enforcement point
267.content: The hub is the only writer of Entitlement and Role state. Apps read (via JWT claim, introspection, or webhook) — they never maintain a parallel copy they write to independently. If an app needs a role concept finer than what App Roles supports, that’s a sign the app needs a new permission defined in its catalog entry, not a local workaround.

268.title: Multi-tenancy
268.content: Three scoping axes. They answer different questions, and are easy to conflate if read too quickly: . | Test vs. live — every table a test-mode credential can write carries test_mode, and a Postgres Row-Level Security policy keyed on a session variable the API sets in every request’s transaction (app.current_test_mode) keeps test and live rows invisible to each other, on both database backends. It fails closed: a transaction that doesn’t set it sees live rows only. This is enforced by the database, not by application WHERE clauses a future query could forget. | organization_id — team grouping. Every record that can belong to an Organization carries it from day one, so it’s never a migration later. | tenant_id — infrastructure placement. Every record scoped to one Application carries it, denormalized from that Application’s own tenant_id (see Tenancy). | . On the shared tier, Organization and Tenant scoping are enforced in the data-access layer: app-confined API keys, owner and org_admin checks, and explicit tenant_id / organization_id filters, each covered by integration tests. They aren’t RLS policies, because a single request legitimately spans many of both: a User in several Organizations, a platform admin listing every Entitlement, a job sweeping every Tenant. An isolated or dedicated_region Tenant’s rows never share a physical cluster with another Tenant’s at all. When the first such Tenant needs a second line of defense inside its own cluster, per-request allowed-set policies (app.allowed_tenant_ids, with an explicit platform bypass) are added then. See Tenant vs. Organization for why these are separate columns.

269.title: Concurrency control
269.content: Entitlement, Role assignment, and Settings writes can race — two support agents acting on the same user, or a webhook retry landing alongside a manual edit. Mutating endpoints on these resources accept an If-Match header carrying the resource’s current version (returned as an ETag on every GET); a write with a stale or missing ETag where one was expected returns 409 with code: "version_conflict" rather than silently applying a last-write-wins update. If-Match is optional on every PATCH/DELETE; without it, the write is last-write-wins. Endpoints where sending it matters most: PATCH /entitlements/{id}, PATCH /users/{id}/apps/{appId}/settings, and PATCH /roles/{id}. Role assignment needs no If-Match, because assign and remove are idempotent set operations that can’t lose an update.

270.title: Transaction boundaries
270.content: Any write described as “also creates” or “also assigns” elsewhere in this spec — most notably POST /users creating a default Profile, Settings, and member Role assignment in one call — is one database transaction. A partial failure (e.g. the Role assignment insert fails) rolls back the whole call; the client sees a single error, not a half-created User. The same rule applies to PATCH /entitlements/{id} and its Audit Event: the state change and the audit record are written together or not at all — an Audit Event that doesn’t actually correspond to a committed change is worse than no Audit Event.

271.title: Audit
271.content: Every state change listed in the Action catalog produces an immutable Audit Event, written in the same transaction as the change: actor (user, API key, or system), action, target, before/after snapshot, request id, and timestamp. Audit events are never deleted or edited through the API, including when the record they describe is later deleted. Two scheduled jobs are the only writers after insert, and both only reduce an event to its shape: the archival job (Audit log lifecycle) and step 4 of the Hard-delete cascade, which redacts before/after. The database enforces this for every caller, including a direct SQL session: a trigger rejects every UPDATE and DELETE on audit_events unless the transaction has set app.audit_maintenance = 'on', which only those two jobs do.

272.title: Idempotency & retries
272.content: Billing webhooks retry. Admin tooling double-clicks. Any mutating endpoint that creates or transitions an Entitlement must accept an Idempotency-Key header and return the original result on a repeated key rather than creating a duplicate. See Conventions.

273.title: Rate limiting
273.content: Per-API-key token bucket, returning 429 with a Retry-After header on exhaustion: . | Scope | Limit | . | Default, all endpoints, per API Key or per User session | 100 requests/minute | . | POST /entitlements, POST /users | 20 requests/minute — tighter, since these are the endpoints scripted abuse would hit first | . | GET /users/{id}/apps/{appId}/effective-permissions, POST /auth/app-tokens, POST /auth/oauth/token | 300 requests/minute — expected to be called on a hot path by downstream apps (see Trust Model), so it’s deliberately not bottlenecked at the default rate | . | POST /auth/login, /signup, /mfa/verify | 10 requests/minute per IP address, in addition to per-account lockout | . | POST /auth/password/forgot, /email/verify/resend | 5 requests/minute per IP address, and 3 per hour per email address | . | POST /auth/token/refresh | 30 requests/minute per session | . | GET /users/{id}/export | 5 per user per day | . | POST /organizations | 10 per user per day | . | POST /applications, self-service | 10 per user per day (staff with applications.manage aren’t limited beyond the default) | . | POST /audit-exports | 20 per API Key or User per day | . | POST /users/{id}/notifications | 600 requests/minute per API Key, and 60 notifications per recipient User per Application per rolling hour (429 rate_limited, details.scope: "recipient"). Platform alerts don’t count toward the per-recipient limit. | . | POST /users/{id}/devices/{deviceId}/test | 10 per device per hour | . Every response carries RateLimit-Limit, RateLimit-Remaining, and RateLimit-Reset (seconds until the bucket refills). A 429 also carries Retry-After. These are starting defaults, not a promise — tune them against real traffic once the API is live, and raise per-key limits for high-volume service integrations (billing) rather than exempting them from limiting entirely. A call made through the MCP Server counts against the same bucket as the REST call it translates to — there’s no separate “MCP traffic” dimension, since it’s the same credential hitting the same underlying endpoint.

274.title: Security logging
274.content: Separate from the Audit log, which records changes to state. The security log records access attempts: every login, failed login, MFA challenge, refresh, refresh-token reuse, lockout, 401, 403, and rate-limit hit. Each entry is structured JSON carrying X-Request-Id, the actor (user id or key id), the IP address, the user agent, and the outcome, and never any token, secret, or password. They go to CloudWatch Logs and are retained for 1 year. A CloudWatch alarm fires on spikes in failed logins, refresh-token reuse, or destructive_operation_restricted. This log is what SOC 2 access-monitoring evidence, and breach scoping under Compliance, come from.

275.title: Service-level objectives
275.content: Targets for the API itself, measured monthly at the API Gateway. They’re published to customers only once there’s a track record, and they aren’t contractual until a business or enterprise agreement says so. | Objective | Target | . | Availability (non-5xx share of requests) | 99.9% | . | effective-permissions, app-tokens, oauth/token latency | p95 < 150 ms, p99 < 400 ms | . | All other endpoints | p95 < 400 ms | . | Webhook dispatch (commit → first attempt) | p95 < 10 s | . | Push notification dispatch (commit → first provider attempt) | p95 < 10 s | . | JWKS availability | 99.99%. JWKS is served by the API with Cache-Control: public, max-age=3600, and Applications cache it for that hour, so a short API outage doesn’t stop token verification. CloudFront goes in front of the whole API domain at the Scale-out trigger, not at Tier 0. | .

276.title: Versioning
276.content: . | The API version is a whole number sent in the Substratal-Version request header, never in the URL. 1 is the only version today, and the header is required (400 api_version_required without it), so no client is ever on a version it didn’t ask for. See Conventions → Versioning. Additive, backward-compatible changes (new optional fields, new endpoints) ship without a version bump. | A breaking change gets the next version number. The old version keeps working for a minimum 6-month deprecation window, announced in the Changelog the day the replacement ships. From then on, every response to a request that names the old version carries a Deprecation header (RFC 9745) and a Sunset header (RFC 8594) giving the retirement date. Once that date passes, the old version is removed from the supported list, and requests naming it get 400 unsupported_api_version. | What counts as breaking: removing or renaming a field, endpoint, or query parameter; changing a field’s type or format; making an optional request field required, or adding a new required one; changing the status code or error code for an existing condition; and changing a default or a behavior that existing callers depend on. Everything else, such as new endpoints, new optional fields, new enum values, and new error codes for new conditions, is additive. | Webhook payloads are versioned independently of the API version, by a date string (api_version, currently 2026-10-05) pinned on each subscription at creation. A breaking payload change ships as a new date. Existing subscriptions keep their pinned shape until their owner moves them forward with PATCH, and old payload versions are supported for at least 12 months. Additive payload fields don’t get a new date. | The MCP Server’s protocol version (negotiated per MCP’s own date-based scheme during initialize) is likewise independent of the API version — a protocol-version bump there doesn’t imply Substratal-Version: 2 here, and vice versa. | Enums can grow new values without a version bump. EntitlementStatus, UserStatus, and similar closed-looking lists in openapi.yaml are allowed to gain new members as additive, non-breaking changes. Clients — and any implementation — must treat an unrecognized enum value as “handle generically / no special case,” never as an error to reject the response over. This is a contract, not just a suggestion: don’t write a switch with no default case against any enum in this spec. | .

277.title: Request tracing
277.content: Every response carries an X-Request-Id (server-generated if the caller didn’t send one in the request). Log it at every layer a request touches. This is what turns “a user says something failed around 2pm” into a specific, searchable trace — cheap to add at the start, expensive to retrofit once there’s production traffic to correlate.

278.title: Testing strategy
278.content: . | Contract tests validate the implementation’s actual responses against openapi.yaml — this is what keeps the machine-readable spec from silently drifting from reality, which is the normal failure mode for hand-maintained API docs. | Unit tests on the Access Control resolution logic (effective_permissions) specifically — it’s the one piece of logic every single request depends on, and it’s pure/deterministic enough to be cheap to test exhaustively (every combination of entitlement status × platform role × app role). | Integration tests run against a real local Postgres (see Deployment Architecture → Local development), not a mocked data layer — the Row-Level Security policies in Multi-tenancy are exactly the kind of thing a mock would let silently pass while actually being broken. | Seed/fixture data for local and test environments should be generated from the same request/response examples already in the API Reference — one source of realistic data, not a second hand-maintained copy that drifts from the docs. | .

279.title: Data retention
279.content: . | Audit Events: retained indefinitely (compliance system of record) — see Audit log lifecycle immediately below for how that stays true without keeping every Audit Event in hot, directly-queryable storage forever. | Disabled/revoked Entitlements: retained, not deleted — re-enabling or investigating a dispute depends on the history. | Notifications: 90 days, then deleted, whatever their read state. Notification delivery results: 30 days. Push devices: deleted 30 days after they become inactive. | Deleted Users: soft-deleted first (status transition), with a separate, deliberate hard-delete process for right-to-erasure requests — see Hard-delete cascade immediately below for what that process actually does, not just that it exists. | . Audit log lifecycle . “Retained indefinitely” and the audit log’s hot-storage window are two different axes, not a contradiction. The hot window is one year for every Tenant; business and enterprise pricing may negotiate a longer one when it ships. | Hot storage. A freshly-written Audit Event lives in the primary audit_events table (Aurora Postgres) with its full before/after snapshot — queryable via API Reference → Audit exactly as specified elsewhere on this page. | Archival, at the end of the hot window. A scheduled job (see Deployment Architecture → Audit log archival) moves every Audit Event older than the hot window out of the hot table: action, timestamp, actor_type/actor_id, target_type/target_id, and every other shape field move to cheap, indefinite cold storage; the before/after snapshot values — the one place the row could hold personal data — are dropped at this point rather than carried forward, the same redaction Hard-delete cascade step 4 already performs for a deleted User, just applied uniformly by age instead of by erasure request. | Cold storage, forever. The shape-only archive is never deleted, satisfying “retained indefinitely” literally — what’s indefinite is the record that something happened, not a guarantee that its full payload stays warm (or stays at all) past the hot window. Retrieving an archived event for a dispute or investigation is a deliberately manual, support-mediated process, not a live API path — see Deployment Architecture for the actual retrieval SLA. | . This is also why the hot/cold split doesn’t weaken Audit trail vs. erasure tension: a snapshot value is gone (not just hidden) the moment it leaves hot storage, for every Tenant, regardless of whether a User ever requests erasure. Hard-delete cascade . Triggered by POST /users/{id}/erasure-requests (see Users) and run by a scheduled job 7 days after the request, well within GDPR Article 12(3)’s 30-day ceiling. The 7-day gap is a window to cancel a request made in error or under account takeover. Soft-delete (the status: deleted transition) happens immediately when the request arrives; this cascade is the follow-up. Runs in this order, each step committed before the next: . | Delete password_hash, mfa_secret, and mfa_pending_secret from every UserIdentity row the User holds, and delete their mfa_recovery_codes. The credential goes, not the row: the row’s method/created_at stays as a record that an identity of that kind existed. Null external_subject_id. | Delete the User’s Profile row outright, and every sessions, refresh_tokens, and auth_tokens row (sessions hold IP addresses and user agents). Delete every Device (push tokens), Notification, and notification delivery the User holds. | For every AppProfile the User holds, set display_handle to null and custom to {}. AppProfile is identity data, so all of it is treated as personal. For every AppSettings row, remove only the keys the Application’s settings_schema marks x-pii: true (see settings_schema rules), and keep structural preferences such as week_start. The rows themselves are retained, since an Application may have a legitimate reason to know an entitlement-shaped record existed. | Redact before/after snapshot values (not the whole row) on every Audit Event where this User is target_user_id. That preserves action/timestamp/actor (the shape of what happened) while removing the one place a deleted field’s value could otherwise still be read back. | Remove the User from every Organization: delete their organization_memberships rows (pending or active), and remove their id from every org-wide Entitlement’s member_overrides. A plain soft-delete leaves both in place, so a restored User comes back exactly as they were. If this removes an Organization’s last active org_admin, its longest-standing active member is promoted, so the Organization is never left unmanageable (the last_org_admin guard can’t apply to a cascade that has to complete). On users: set email to erased+<id>@invalid.substratal, null pending_email, and keep status: deleted. The row must survive as the foreign-key target of the history in step 6. | Leave Entitlement rows (and their opaque order_id) in place, pseudonymized by the steps above having removed the identifying data they’d otherwise join against. They’re retained under a legitimate-interest basis (financial/business records) distinct from, and not overridden by, the erasure right. | Mark the erasure_requests row completed and write user.erased (actor system). | . Each step is idempotent, so a failed run resumes safely from the start. GET /users/{id}/export (see API Reference → Users) reads every table this cascade writes to, plus one it deliberately doesn’t: global Settings. Export answers “what do you have on me,” so it includes everything keyed to the User. Erasure answers “stop having anything that identifies you,” and global Settings (locale, timezone, theme, notifications) identifies no one once the User’s email, Profile, and credentials are gone, so the row stays as a pseudonymous preference record. Every other table is symmetric: if export shows it, the cascade clears it.

280.title: Availability expectations on the trust model
280.content: Because downstream apps verify access against this API (see Trust Model), this API’s availability is a dependency of every app in the catalog, not just the hub dashboard. JWT verification keeps apps functioning through a brief hub outage; live introspection calls do not. This is a reason to lean on JWTs for routine checks and reserve introspection for genuinely sensitive actions, independent of the latency tradeoff discussed on that page.

281.title: Notifications
281.content: The records behind push notifications and the notification inbox. See API Reference → Push Notifications for the endpoints and the delivery rules. | Why these live in the hub | Device . | Example | Lifecycle | . | PushCredential | Notification . | NotificationDelivery | . | How they relate | Privacy and retention | .

282.title: Why these live in the hub
282.content: Every Application needs to reach its users with alerts and updates, and every one would otherwise build the same machinery: a table of device tokens, the APNs and FCM integrations, token cleanup, retries, a “what did I miss” list, and per-user mute switches. The hub already knows who the User is, which Applications they can reach, which session each install belongs to, and what they’ve muted (the push channel in Settings). So the hub owns that machinery once, and an Application sends a notification with one API call. What stays with the Application is what has to: its own provider credentials, because Apple and Google deliver only for the app a token was issued to, and the decision about what to say and when.

283.title: Device
283.content: One install of one Application, on one device, signed in as one User, with the provider token that reaches it. | Field | Type | Notes | . | id | string | dvc_ prefix. | . | user_id | string | The User signed in on the install. | . | application_id | string | The Application the install belongs to. The same phone running two Applications is two Devices, because the OS issues each app its own token. | . | provider | enum | apns | fcm | web_push. | . | environment | enum, nullable | production | sandbox. Set only for apns, where it picks Apple’s production or development gateway. | . | token_hint | string | The last four characters of the token. The token itself (or, for web_push, the whole PushSubscription) is stored KMS-encrypted and never returned. | . | name, app_version | string, nullable | Labels the client supplies, for the User’s own device list and for support. | . | session_id | string, nullable | The Session that registered the device. Revoking that session deactivates it. null when an app key registered it. | . | status | enum | active | inactive. Only active devices are sent to. | . | inactive_reason | enum, nullable | Set exactly when status is inactive: unregistered (the provider reported the token gone), session_revoked, user_suspended, user_deleted, test_user_expired (a test-mode User’s expires_at passed), stale (not re-registered for 270 days), limit (displaced by a 21st device), or credential_removed (a web_push device whose VAPID key was deleted). | . | last_registered_at | timestamp | The latest registration or refresh. | . | last_delivery_at | timestamp, nullable | The latest delivery a provider accepted. | . | test_mode | boolean |   | . | created_at, updated_at | timestamp |   | . A Device is identified by its token, not by anything the client chooses: one Device per (Application, provider, token) and mode. Registering a token again refreshes the same Device. Registering it as a different User replaces the Device, so one User’s device history never passes to the next person to sign in on that install. Example . { "id": "dvc_01JAH2B3C4D5E6F7G8H9J0K1M2", "user_id": "usr_01JAG3Z9X8QS3F6K2M4N5P6R7S", "application_id": "app_timetrack", "provider": "apns", "environment": "production", "token_hint": "…9f3a", "name": "Jordan's iPhone", "app_version": "2.4.0", "session_id": "ses_01JAG8K4Q9R0S1T2V3V4W5X6Y8", "status": "active", "inactive_reason": null, "last_registered_at": "2026-10-17T15:05:00Z", "last_delivery_at": "2026-10-17T15:10:02Z", "test_mode": false, "created_at": "2026-10-17T15:05:00Z", "updated_at": "2026-10-17T15:10:02Z" } . Lifecycle . register (POST) ──► active ──── logout / session revoked ──────────► inactive ▲ ├─── provider reports token gone ──────► │ │ ├─── user suspended or deleted ────────► │ │ ├─── 270 days without re-registering ──► │ │ └─── displaced by a 21st device ───────► │ │ │ └──────── re-register the same token ◄───────────┤ ▼ deleted: DELETE, the token registered by another User, or 30 days after deactivation .

284.title: PushCredential
284.content: An Application’s credential for one push provider. Configuration, not per-user data: like the Application row it belongs to, it’s shared by test and live mode. | Field | Type | Notes | . | id | string | pcr_ prefix. Addressed in the API by provider (/applications/{id}/push-credentials/{provider}), since there’s at most one per provider. The id is what Audit Events reference. | . | application_id | string |   | . | provider | enum | apns | fcm | web_push. Unique per Application. | . | team_id, key_id, topic | string | APNs only. topic is the app’s bundle id. | . | project_id, client_email | string | FCM only, read from the service account. | . | subject, vapid_public_key | string | Web Push only. The platform generates the VAPID key pair. The public key is what a web client subscribes with. | . | (secret) | write-only | The APNs .p8 key, the FCM service-account JSON, or the VAPID private key. KMS-encrypted at rest, never returned, never in an Audit Event. | . | status | enum | active | failed. failed when the provider rejects the credential itself. Sends to that provider skip until it’s fixed. | . | failure_reason, failed_at | string / timestamp, nullable | The provider’s reason code and when it failed. | . | last_used_at | timestamp, nullable |   | . | created_at, updated_at | timestamp |   | . Managed only by a person (the Application’s owner, or applications.manage), never by an API Key, the same rule as API Keys: it’s a credential, and credentials are managed by people. Every create, change, and removal is audited.

285.title: Notification
285.content: One message to one User, from one Application or from the platform. It’s both the unit of sending and the inbox item. | Field | Type | Notes | . | id | string | ntf_ prefix. | . | user_id | string | The recipient. | . | application_id | string, nullable | The sending Application. null for a platform alert. | . | source | enum | application | platform. platform exactly when application_id is null. | . | category | string | What kind of notification it is, in the sender’s own vocabulary (timesheet.reminder). security., account., and billing. are reserved for the platform catalog. | . | priority | enum | normal | high. | . | title, body | string | body is nullable. | . | data | object | Up to 20 string → string pairs, delivered with the push and kept with the inbox item. | . | action_url | string, nullable | Where opening it takes the User. | . | badge, sound, collapse_key, ttl_seconds |   | Push presentation and delivery hints. See Sending a notification. | . | push | object | requested, status (queued | sent | failed | skipped), devices_targeted, devices_sent, devices_failed, and skip_reason. A summary of the deliveries below. | . | state | enum | unread | read | archived, derived from read_at and archived_at. | . | read_at, archived_at | timestamp, nullable |   | . | sender | object | { "type": "api_key" \| "user" \| "system", "id": … }, the same actor shape as an Audit Event. | . | test_mode | boolean |   | . | created_at, updated_at | timestamp |   | . Kept for 90 days, then deleted by a nightly job, whatever its state. The inbox is a recent-activity list, not an archive. Sending a notification is not an Audit Event: it changes no access, and the Notification row, with its sender, is already the record of who sent what. NotificationDelivery . One attempt to reach one Device with one Notification: the outbox row a worker picks up, and the per-device result afterwards. | Field | Type | Notes | . | id | string | ndl_ prefix. | . | notification_id | string |   | . | device_id | string, nullable | null once the Device is deleted. | . | provider | enum | Copied from the Device when the delivery is created. | . | status | enum | pending | sent | failed | skipped. | . | attempts | integer | 0–4. | . | error | string, nullable | The provider’s reason code (BadDeviceToken, UNREGISTERED, …) or timeout. | . | sent_at | timestamp, nullable | When the provider accepted it. | . Deliveries are written in the same transaction as their Notification, one per Device eligible at that moment, so a committed send can’t lose its push. They’re kept for 30 days.

287.title: Privacy and retention
287.content: Device tokens, notification content, and delivery results are personal data: . | GET /users/{id}/export includes the User’s devices (without tokens) and their notifications. | The hard-delete cascade deletes every Device, Notification, and NotificationDelivery of the User. | A soft-delete or suspension deactivates the User’s devices right away, so nothing is pushed to a closed or suspended account. | . The payload of every push passes through Apple, Google, or a browser vendor’s push service, which is why Compliance lists them as sub-processors, and why senders should keep sensitive content out of the title, body, and data. Building the tables? See Database Schema → Push notifications.

288.title: Push Notifications
288.content: How alerts and other updates reach a User: on their devices through Apple Push Notification service (APNs), Firebase Cloud Messaging (FCM), and Web Push, and in an inbox their client reads through this API. See Domain Model → Notifications for the entities, and Webhooks for the separate, server-to-server channel that tells an Application about changes. | How it fits together | Endpoints | Push credentials . | POST /applications/{id}/push-credentials | GET /applications/{id}/push-credentials, GET …/{provider} | PATCH /applications/{id}/push-credentials/{provider} | DELETE /applications/{id}/push-credentials/{provider} | . | Devices . | POST /users/{id}/devices | GET /users/{id}/devices | PATCH /users/{id}/devices/{deviceId} | DELETE /users/{id}/devices/{deviceId} | POST /users/{id}/devices/{deviceId}/test | . | Sending a notification . | POST /users/{id}/notifications | Preferences | Rate limits | . | The inbox . | GET /users/{id}/notifications | GET /users/{id}/notifications/{notificationId} | PATCH /users/{id}/notifications/{notificationId} | POST /users/{id}/notifications/mark-read | GET /users/{id}/notifications/unread-count | . | Platform alerts | What a device receives | Delivery | Sessions and device lifecycle | Test mode | Webhook events | Errors specific to this resource | . Specified 2026-10-17 and implemented 2026-10-18 (Changelog). Its defaults are settled: platform alerts push only through Applications that opt in, sending is one User per call (no broadcast yet), each recipient gets at most 60 notifications per Application per hour, the inbox keeps 90 days, the notifications.push channel is the only preference, and the push providers are sub-processors.

289.title: How it fits together
289.content: Four pieces, each owned by a different party: . | Piece | What it is | Who writes it | . | Push credential | An Application’s own APNs key, FCM service account, or Web Push (VAPID) key pair. Push providers deliver only for the app that holds these, so every Application brings its own. | The Application’s owner | . | Device | One install of an Application on one device, signed in as one User, plus the provider token that reaches it. | The User’s client, or the Application’s backend | . | Notification | One message to one User: a title, a body, optional data, and how urgent it is. | The Application’s backend (app-scoped key), or the platform itself for platform alerts | . | Inbox | Every notification a User has received, with read and archived state, readable through the API whether or not the push itself arrived. | The User’s client marks items read or archived | . A send writes the Notification and one delivery per eligible device in a single transaction, the same outbox pattern webhooks use. A worker then hands each delivery to the provider. A device a provider reports as gone is deactivated automatically, so a send never keeps targeting a dead token. Push is a notification channel, not an access-control mechanism. It never grants or revokes anything, and an Application still meets the immediate-revocation requirement through access.revoked webhooks, not pushes.
