/applications/{id}/push-credentials/{provider} | as for the list | Fetch one provider’s configuration. | . | PATCH | /applications/{id}/push-credentials/{provider} | the owner or applications.manage, with a User token | Replace key material, change non-secret fields, or re-enable a failed credential. | . | DELETE | /applications/{id}/push-credentials/{provider} | the owner or applications.manage, with a User token | Remove a provider. | . | GET | /users/{id}/devices | self, the app’s own key, or users.list | List a User’s devices. | . | POST | /users/{id}/devices | self or the app’s own key | Register a device, or refresh an existing registration. | . | GET | /users/{id}/devices/{deviceId} | self, the app’s own key, or users.list | Fetch one device. | . | PATCH | /users/{id}/devices/{deviceId} | self or the app’s own key | Update a device’s name, app version, or rotated token. | . | DELETE | /users/{id}/devices/{deviceId} | self, the app’s own key, or users.manage | Unregister a device. | . | POST | /users/{id}/devices/{deviceId}/test | self or the app’s own key | Send a test push to one device and wait for the provider’s answer. | . | POST | /users/{id}/notifications | the app’s own key with notifications.send, or platform notifications.send | Send one notification to one User. | . | GET | /users/{id}/notifications | self, the app’s own key, or users.list | List the User’s inbox. | . | GET | /users/{id}/notifications/unread-count | self or the app’s own key | Count unread notifications. | . | POST | /users/{id}/notifications/mark-read | self or the app’s own key | Mark many notifications read at once. | . | GET | /users/{id}/notifications/{notificationId} | self, the app’s own key, or users.list | Fetch one notification, with its per-device delivery results. | . | PATCH | /users/{id}/notifications/{notificationId} | self or the app’s own key | Mark one notification read, unread, or archived. | . “The app’s own key” means any app-scoped API Key scoped to that Application, as on Settings. An app key only ever sees its own Application’s push credentials, devices, and notifications. Anything else returns 404, as though it didn’t exist. It never sees platform alerts, which belong to the User. {id} may be me for a User token (see Conventions → me). Two ways a client reaches these endpoints. An Application using embedded login holds a platform access token and calls the /users/me/… endpoints directly. An Application using the hosted flow holds only app tokens, which this API doesn’t accept as a Bearer credential, so its client hands the provider token to its own backend, which registers the device with its app key. Both paths produce the same Device. The only difference is that a device registered by an app key isn’t tied to a session.

291.title: Push credentials
291.content:
APNs, FCM, and browser push services deliver a push only when the sender proves it’s the app the token was issued to. So each Application configures its own credentials, and the platform signs every request to the provider with them. There’s at most one credential per provider per Application. Push credentials are Application configuration, shared by test and live mode the same way the Application row itself is. Test-mode notifications reach only test-mode devices, but they use the same credentials. APNs development builds are handled per device, by environment: sandbox, not by a separate credential. POST /applications/{id}/push-credentials . // Request — APNs, token-based authentication with a .p8 key { "provider": "apns", "team_id": "ABCDE12345", "key_id": "XYZ987WVU6", "topic": "com.substratal.timetrack", "private_key": "-----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----
MIGTAgEAMBMGByqGSM49AgEGCCqGSM49AwEHBHkwdwIBAQQg...
-----END PRIVATE KEY-----
" } . // Request — FCM, HTTP v1 API with a service account { "provider": "fcm", "service_account": { "type": "service_account", "project_id": "timetrack-prod", "private_key_id": "3f1c...", "private_key": "-----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----
...
-----END PRIVATE KEY-----
", "client_email": "push-sender@timetrack-prod.iam.gserviceaccount.com" } } . // Request — Web Push. The platform generates the VAPID key pair. { "provider": "web_push", "subject": "mailto:push@timetrack.substratalapps.com" } . // Response — 201 (APNs) { "id": "pcr_01JAH1A2B3C4D5E6F7G8H9J0K1", "application_id": "app_timetrack", "provider": "apns", "status": "active", "team_id": "ABCDE12345", "key_id": "XYZ987WVU6", "topic": "com.substratal.timetrack", "failure_reason": null, "failed_at": null, "last_used_at": null, "created_at": "2026-10-17T15:00:00Z", "updated_at": "2026-10-17T15:00:00Z" } . | Provider | Required | Returned (never the secret) | . | apns | team_id (10 characters), key_id (10 characters), topic (the app’s bundle id), private_key (the .p8 file’s contents: a PEM PKCS#8 P-256 key) | team_id, key_id, topic | . | fcm | service_account (the downloaded JSON key, with type: service_account, project_id, private_key, and client_email) | project_id, client_email | . | web_push | subject (a mailto: or https: contact URI, sent to browser push services per RFC 8292) | subject, vapid_public_key (base64url, uncompressed P-256 point) | . | private_key, service_account, and the generated VAPID private key are write-only. They’re stored KMS-encrypted, never returned by any endpoint, and never written to an Audit Event, the same treatment as a webhook signing secret. | The material is checked for shape on write (the key parses, the JSON has the required fields), and a failure is 422 invalid_push_credential. It isn’t checked against the provider, because that would make the request depend on Apple’s or Google’s availability. Use POST …/devices/{deviceId}/test to prove it end to end. | vapid_public_key is what a web client passes as applicationServerKey to PushManager.subscribe(). The app’s own key can read it, so a web client can fetch it from its backend. | A second credential for the same provider is 409 push_credential_exists. Use PATCH to replace it. | Writes push_credential.created. | . Credential management is always done by a person, the same rule as API Keys. An API Key, including the Application’s own, can read credentials but never create, change, or remove them (400 user_token_required). GET /applications/{id}/push-credentials, GET …/{provider} . The list returns every configured provider as { "data": [ … ] } with no pagination, since there are at most three. {provider} is apns, fcm, or web_push. status is one of: . | active. | failed, after the provider rejected the credential itself (APNs 403 InvalidProviderToken, FCM 401/403). failure_reason holds the provider’s reason code and failed_at when it happened. Sends to that provider’s devices are skipped with skip_reason: credential_failed until the credential is fixed, the owner is emailed, and a push_credential.failed webhook fires. | . PATCH /applications/{id}/push-credentials/{provider} . // Request — rotate the APNs key { "key_id": "NEWKEY1234", "private_key": "-----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----
...
-----END PRIVATE KEY-----
" } . Writable: the same fields as on POST for that provider, plus status (only failed → active). Any change to key material also returns a failed credential to active. provider and application_id are fixed (422 read_only_field). The VAPID key pair can’t be rotated in place, because every existing browser subscription is bound to it. Delete and recreate the credential instead. Writes push_credential.updated. Returns 200 with the credential. DELETE /applications/{id}/push-credentials/{provider} . 204. Pending deliveries to that provider are skipped (each delivery’s error is credential_removed), and new sends skip the provider (skip_reason: no_credentials when no other provider can reach the User). Devices are kept, because an APNs or FCM token stays valid and works again once a credential is configured. The exception is web_push: browser subscriptions are bound to the deleted VAPID key, so every web_push device of the Application becomes inactive with inactive_reason: credential_removed. Writes push_credential.deleted. Destructive. See MCP Server → Tool annotations.

292.title: Devices
292.content: A Device is one install of one Application, signed in as one User, with the provider token that reaches it. The same phone running two Applications is two Devices, because each app gets its own token from the OS. POST /users/{id}/devices . Called on every app launch and whenever the OS issues a new token, so registration is an idempotent upsert, not a one-time create. // Request — iOS { "application_id": "app_timetrack", "provider": "apns", "token": "7f3c9a1e2b4d6f8a0c2e4b6d8f0a2c4e6b8d0f2a4c6e8b0d2f4a6c8e0b2d9f3a", "environment": "production", "name": "Jordan's iPhone", "app_version": "2.4.0" } . // Request — a browser, with the PushSubscription from PushManager.subscribe() { "application_id": "app_timetrack", "provider": "web_push", "subscription": { "endpoint": "https://fcm.googleapis.com/fcm/send/eHk3...:APA91b...", "keys": { "p256dh": "BNcRdreALRFXTkOOUHK1EtK2wtaz5Ry4YfYCA_0QTpQtUbVlUls0VJXg7A8u-Ts1XbjhazAkj7I99e8QcYP7DkM", "auth": "tBHItJI5svbpez7KI4CCXg" } }, "name": "Chrome on macOS" } . // Response — 201 for a new registration, 200 for a refresh of an existing one { "id": "dvc_01JAH2B3C4D5E6F7G8H9J0K1M2", "user_id": "usr_01JAG3Z9X8QS3F6K2M4N5P6R7S", "application_id": "app_timetrack", "provider": "apns", "environment": "production", "token_hint": "…9f3a", "name": "Jordan's iPhone", "app_version": "2.4.0", "session_id": "ses_01JAG8K4Q9R0S1T2V3V4W5X6Y8", "status": "active", "inactive_reason": null, "last_registered_at": "2026-10-17T15:05:00Z", "last_delivery_at": null, "test_mode": false, "created_at": "2026-10-17T15:05:00Z", "updated_at": "2026-10-17T15:05:00Z" } . | Field | Rules | . | application_id | Required. The User must have active access to it right now (allow()), otherwise 403 entitlement_required. An app key may only pass its own Application. | . | provider | Required. apns, fcm, or web_push. No credential needs to exist yet. A device registered before its credential is configured simply isn’t reachable until it is. | . | token | Required for apns (the device token as hex, 64–200 characters) and fcm (the registration token, 1–4,096 characters). Not allowed for web_push. | . | subscription | Required for web_push, and only for it: endpoint (an https URL on a public host, the same SSRF rules as a webhook URL) and keys.p256dh and keys.auth (base64url). | . | environment | apns only, required: production or sandbox (a development build, delivered through api.sandbox.push.apple.com). | . | name, app_version | Optional labels, up to 100 and 50 characters, for the User’s own device list and for support. | . A malformed token or subscription is 422 invalid_device_token. What makes a registration “the same” device is the token: one Device per (application_id, provider, token) and mode, where a web_push device’s token is its endpoint. Registering an existing token: . | for the same User refreshes it and returns 200. last_registered_at moves forward, name, app_version, and environment take the new values, and session_id becomes the caller’s current session (null when an app key registers it). An inactive device becomes active again and fires device.registered. | for a different User (someone else signed in on that install) deletes the previous registration and creates a new Device for the caller (201). A device never carries one User’s history over to another. The previous owner’s Device is gone, and device.deleted fires for it. | . The token itself is never returned. It’s stored KMS-encrypted, and responses carry only token_hint, its last four characters. Device tokens aren’t bearer credentials, but they are personal data, and a client never needs to read one back. At most 20 active devices per User per Application. Registering a 21st deactivates the one registered longest ago (inactive_reason: limit). Self-service and app-key registrations write no Audit Event. They’re ordinary account activity, the same as a login. GET /users/{id}/devices . // Response — 200 { "data": [ { "id": "dvc_01JAH2B3C4D5E6F7G8H9J0K1M2", "application_id": "app_timetrack", "provider": "apns", "status": "active", "...": "..." } ], "page": { "next_cursor": null, "has_more": false } } . Filters: application_id, provider, status, and include_inactive=true. Without an explicit status or include_inactive, only active devices are listed, per Conventions → Filtering. An app key gets only its own Application’s devices, whatever it passes. PATCH /users/{id}/devices/{deviceId} . // Request — the OS rotated the token { "token": "9a8b7c6d5e4f3a2b1c0d9e8f7a6b5c4d3e2f1a0b9c8d7e6f5a4b3c2d1e0f9a8b", "app_version": "2.5.0" } . Writable: name, app_version, environment (apns), and the token (token, or subscription for web_push). If the new token is already registered as another Device of the same User and Application, that other registration is deleted, so one token never maps to two Devices. Writing a token reactivates an inactive device. application_id, provider, user_id, session_id, and status are read-only (422 read_only_field). Returns 200 with the Device. DELETE /users/{id}/devices/{deviceId} . 204. Hard delete: the Device is removed, its pending deliveries are dropped, and device.deleted fires. Call this when the User turns notifications off in the app, or from the app’s own sign-out if it registered the device with its app key. users.manage can delete anyone’s device, which writes device.deleted to the audit log. Self-service and app-key deletes aren’t audited. Destructive. POST /users/{id}/devices/{deviceId}/test . // Request — optional overrides { "title": "Test notification", "body": "If you can see this, push works." } . // Response — 200 { "device_id": "dvc_01JAH2B3C4D5E6F7G8H9J0K1M2", "status": "sent", "provider_status": 200, "error": null, "duration_ms": 184 } . Sends one push to one device through the real signing and delivery path, waits up to 10 seconds for the provider’s answer, and returns it. status is sent or failed, and error carries the provider’s reason code (for example BadDeviceToken, UNREGISTERED, or InvalidProviderToken) when there is one. It’s for proving a credential and a device work together while integrating. | title defaults to Test notification from Substratal and body to null. | It’s sent whatever the User’s push preference says (you asked for it), and to an inactive device too, so you can check a device the platform deactivated. | It isn’t stored in the inbox and doesn’t count toward the per-recipient limit. It has its own limit of 10 per device per hour, on top of the default per-key bucket. Its result updates the device and credential the same way a real delivery would: an invalid token deactivates the device, and a rejected credential marks it failed. | 409 push_not_configured if the Application has no credential for the device’s provider. | .

293.title: Sending a notification
293.content: POST /users/{id}/notifications . // Request { "category": "timesheet.reminder", "priority": "normal", "title": "Timesheet due tomorrow", "body": "Your timesheet for the week of Oct 12 is due Friday at 5 pm.", "data": { "timesheet_id": "ts_8841" }, "action_url": "com.substratal.timetrack:/timesheets/ts_8841", "badge": 1, "sound": "default", "collapse_key": "timesheet-due-2026-10-12", "ttl_seconds": 86400 } . // Response — 201 { "id": "ntf_01JAH3C4D5E6F7G8H9J0K1M2N3", "user_id": "usr_01JAG3Z9X8QS3F6K2M4N5P6R7S", "application_id": "app_timetrack", "source": "application", "category": "timesheet.reminder", "priority": "normal", "title": "Timesheet due tomorrow", "body": "Your timesheet for the week of Oct 12 is due Friday at 5 pm.", "data": { "timesheet_id": "ts_8841" }, "action_url": "com.substratal.timetrack:/timesheets/ts_8841", "badge": 1, "sound": "default", "collapse_key": "timesheet-due-2026-10-12", "ttl_seconds": 86400, "push": { "requested": true, "status": "queued", "devices_targeted": 2, "devices_sent": 0, "devices_failed": 0, "skip_reason": null }, "state": "unread", "read_at": null, "archived_at": null, "sender": { "type": "api_key", "id": "key_01JAGE5F6G7H8J9K011M2N304P" }, "test_mode": false, "created_at": "2026-10-17T15:10:00Z", "updated_at": "2026-10-17T15:10:00Z" } . The caller is the Application’s own key with notifications.send (an app-confined permission), and the notification is from that Application. A platform key or User holding platform notifications.send may send on behalf of any Application by passing application_id. Platform alerts aren’t sent through this endpoint. The platform raises them itself (see Platform alerts). | Field | Rules | . | title | Required. 1–120 characters. | . | body | Optional. Up to 1,000 characters. | . | category | Required. What kind of notification this is, for the client’s grouping, actions, and filters: 1–64 characters matching ^[a-z][a-z0-9_]*(\.[a-z0-9_]+)*$. The Application chooses its own vocabulary. The prefixes security., account., and billing. are reserved for platform alerts (422 reserved_category). | . | priority | normal (default) or high. high is for time-sensitive alerts the User needs now. It maps to each provider’s urgent delivery class, and providers throttle apps that overuse it. normal is for other updates. | . | push | Boolean, default true. false writes the notification to the inbox without a push: an update the User should see next time they look, not one that should buzz their phone. | . | data | Optional. Up to 20 keys, each string → string, 2 KB serialized. Delivered to the app with the push and stored with the inbox item. String values only, because FCM’s data payload only carries strings. The key substratal is reserved. | . | action_url | Optional. Where the client should take the User when they open it: an https URL or a private-use URI scheme, the same formats as redirect_uris. Up to 2,048 characters. | . | badge | Optional integer, 0–99,999, for the app icon badge (APNs) or notification count (FCM). null leaves the badge alone. | . | sound | default or null (silent). Defaults to default for high priority and null for normal. | . | collapse_key | Optional. Up to 64 characters of [A-Za-z0-9._-]. A newer notification with the same key replaces an older one still waiting on the device or provider, so the User sees one current status instead of a stack. It doesn’t change the inbox, where both stay. | . | ttl_seconds | How long the provider should keep trying to reach an offline device: 0–2,419,200 (28 days), default 86,400. 0 means deliver now or not at all. It doesn’t affect how long the notification stays in the inbox. | . | application_id | Only for a platform notifications.send caller, and required for one. An app key’s sends are always from its own Application. | . The whole push payload must fit in 4 KB, the limit all three providers share, after the platform adds its own substratal block (see What a device receives). A request that doesn’t fit is 422 notification_too_large, with details.bytes and details.max. The recipient must have active access to the Application right now (allow() passes, which also requires the User to be active), otherwise 403 entitlement_required. A User who has lost access to an app stops hearing from it at the same moment, whatever the sender believes. Accepts an optional Idempotency-Key, honored as in Conventions → Idempotency. Send one whenever the send is triggered by an event your backend might process twice, such as a queue message, so a retry doesn’t buzz the User’s phone twice. A send always creates the notification, even when no push goes out. The response is 201 either way, and push.status says what happened to the push: . | push.status | Meaning | . | queued | Deliveries are on their way to devices_targeted devices. | . | sent | At least one provider accepted it. devices_sent and devices_failed count the outcome per device. “Accepted” means the provider took it, not that the User saw it: neither APNs nor FCM reports display. | . | failed | Every targeted device failed. | . | skipped | No push was attempted. skip_reason says why. | . skip_reason is one of: . | push_not_requested: the request set push: false. | push_disabled: the User turned push off, globally or for this Application (see Preferences). | no_devices: the User has no active device for this Application. | no_credentials: the Application has no credential for any provider the User’s devices use. | credential_failed: the matching credentials are all failed. | expired: ttl_seconds ran out before any attempt could be made. | . The notification is in the User’s inbox in every case. That’s what makes the inbox a reliable place to check, and what lets an Application fall back to another channel when a push can’t go out (see notification.push_failed). Preferences . There’s no separate preferences resource. Push follows the push channel in the User’s existing Settings notifications map, resolved per Application: . | A resolved notifications.push of false, from global Settings or from this Application’s AppSettings override, means no push for this Application. The inbox still gets the notification, with skip_reason: push_disabled. | A missing push key counts as on. Registering a device follows the User granting the OS’s own notification permission, which is the real opt-in. | . The OS-level permission stays the User’s final word. If they revoke it on the device, the provider reports the token invalid on the next send, and the platform deactivates the device. Rate limits . Two limits, on top of the default per-key bucket: . | Per sender: 600 sends per minute per API Key. | Per recipient: 60 notifications per User per Application per rolling hour. Platform alerts don’t count toward it. A send over the limit is 429 rate_limited with details.scope: "recipient", so a bug in one Application’s backend can’t flood one person’s phone. | .

294.title: The inbox
294.content: Every notification a User receives is kept for 90 days, whether or not its push arrived, so a client can always show what the User missed. A client renders it from these endpoints and keeps it in step with what the User does. GET /users/{id}/notifications . // Response — 200 { "data": [ { "id": "ntf_01JAH3C4D5E6F7G8H9J0K1M2N3", "application_id": "app_timetrack", "source": "application", "category": "timesheet.reminder", "priority": "normal", "title": "Timesheet due tomorrow", "body": "Your timesheet for the week of Oct 12 is due Friday at 5 pm.", "action_url": "com.substratal.timetrack:/timesheets/ts_8841", "state": "unread", "created_at": "2026-10-17T15:10:00Z", "...": "..." } ], "page": { "next_cursor": null, "has_more": false } } . Newest first. Filters: state (unread, read, archived), application_id, source (application or platform), category, priority, created_after, created_before, and include_inactive=true. Archived notifications are excluded unless the caller passes state=archived or include_inactive=true, the same rule as other terminal states in Conventions → Filtering. Who sees what: . | The User themself sees everything addressed to them: every Application’s notifications and every platform alert. | An app key sees only its own Application’s notifications. The application_id filter is forced, and source=platform returns nothing. | users.list (support) can read any User’s inbox, for investigations. | . GET /users/{id}/notifications/{notificationId} . The full Notification, as in the send response, plus deliveries, one entry per targeted device: . { "id": "ntf_01JAH3C4D5E6F7G8H9J0K1M2N3", "push": { "requested": true, "status": "sent", "devices_targeted": 2, "devices_sent": 1, "devices_failed": 1, "skip_reason": null }, "deliveries": [ { "id": "ndl_01JAH3D4E5F6G7H8J9K0M1N2P3", "device_id": "dvc_01JAH2B3C4D5E6F7G8H9J0K1M2", "provider": "apns", "status": "sent", "attempts": 1, "error": null, "sent_at": "2026-10-17T15:10:02Z" }, { "id": "ndl_01JAH3D4E5F6G7H8J9K0M1N2P4", "device_id": null, "provider": "fcm", "status": "failed", "attempts": 1, "error": "UNREGISTERED", "sent_at": null } ], "...": "..." } . device_id is null once that Device has been deleted. Delivery details are kept for 30 days, after which deliveries is [] and only the push summary remains. PATCH /users/{id}/notifications/{notificationId} . // Request { "state": "read" } . state is the only writable field. Every transition is allowed: . | To | Effect | . | read | Sets read_at (or keeps it). From archived, also clears archived_at. | . | unread | Clears read_at and archived_at. | . | archived | Sets archived_at, and read_at too if it was unset. The notification leaves the default list. | . Returns 200 with the Notification. No Audit Event: this is the User’s own reading state, not an access change. POST /users/{id}/notifications/mark-read . // Request — everything from TimeTrack up to a point in time { "application_id": "app_timetrack", "before": "2026-10-17T15:10:00Z" } . // Response — 200 { "updated_count": 4 } . Marks every unread notification matching the filters as read. Each filter is optional: application_id, source, category, and before (only notifications created at or before this time, so items that arrive while the User is looking aren’t swept up). An empty body marks everything the caller can see. An app key’s application_id is forced to its own. GET /users/{id}/notifications/unread-count . // Response — 200 { "unread_count": 3, "applications": [ { "application_id": "app_timetrack", "unread_count": 2 }, { "application_id": null, "unread_count": 1 } ] } . Unread, unarchived notifications. application_id: null is the platform alerts. Accepts the application_id and source filters. An app key gets only its own Application’s count. A client typically calls it on launch and after handling a push, to set its badge.

295.title: Platform alerts
295.content: The platform raises a small, fixed set of notifications itself, about the User’s account rather than any one Application. They use the same Notification object, with source: platform, application_id: null, sender: {"type": "system", "id": "system"}, and a category from this catalog: . | category | priority | Raised when | data | . | security.new_sign_in | high | A login creates a session from a user agent not seen in the User’s sessions during the last 90 days. A User’s first session, at signup, raises nothing. | session_id, user_agent, ip_address | . | security.password_changed | high | POST /users/{id}/password, or a password reset. | — | . | security.email_changed | high | An email change completes. | — | . | security.mfa_disabled | high | TOTP is turned off by the User, or reset by support. | — | . | security.session_reuse_detected | high | A reused refresh token revokes a session (refresh_token_reused). | session_id | . | account.organization_invitation | normal | A pending membership is created for an existing User (Organizations → Adding members). | organization_id, invited_by | . | account.access_granted | normal | The User gains resolved access to an Application (the same moment access.granted fires). Raised only for access a developer or admin grants (purchase, trial, admin_grant, or org_seat), never for platform-managed free or subscription Entitlements: signing up, subscribing to Standard, or a new free Application would otherwise push one alert per app. Also not raised within 60 seconds of signup. | application_id | . billing. categories are reserved for subscription alerts, such as a failed payment. None are sent yet; Stripe emails the customer directly. These run alongside the emails the platform already sends for the same events, and don’t replace them. A User who has never registered a device still gets the email. Which devices get a platform alert’s push. A device belongs to an Application, and only an Application’s own credentials can reach it. So a platform alert is pushed only to devices of Applications that have opted in with receives_platform_notifications: true, typically a first-party Substratal app. Without that, a platform alert goes to the inbox (and the email above) but makes no push, and skip_reason is no_devices. Opting in is the owner’s choice, because the alert arrives under that app’s name and icon. The push preference applies per device, resolved for that device’s Application. Targets are chosen when the alert is raised. An action that also revokes sessions, such as a password reset or a detected token reuse, raises its alert before the revocation in the same transaction. The User’s devices still get the warning, even though they’re about to be signed out. That exception applies only to security.* alerts. Any other pending delivery to a device that has since become inactive is skipped. Platform alerts never reach an Application through webhooks, and an app key can’t list them. They’re between the platform and the User.

296.title: What a device receives
296.content: The platform builds each provider’s payload from the Notification. Every payload carries a substratal block, so the app can match the push to its inbox item and mark it read: . { "substratal": { "notification_id": "ntf_01JAH3C4D5E6F7G8H9J0K1M2N3", "application_id": "app_timetrack", "source": "application", "category": "timesheet.reminder", "action_url": "com.substratal.timetrack:/timesheets/ts_8841" } } . | Notification field | APNs | FCM (HTTP v1) | Web Push | . | title, body | aps.alert.title, aps.alert.body | message.notification.title, .body | In the encrypted JSON payload | . | priority: high / normal | apns-priority: 10 with aps.interruption-level: time-sensitive / apns-priority: 5 with active | android.priority: HIGH / NORMAL | Urgency: high / normal | . | ttl_seconds | apns-expiration | android.ttl | TTL header | . | collapse_key | apns-collapse-id | android.collapse_key | Topic header | . | badge | aps.badge | android.notification.notification_count | In the payload | . | sound | aps.sound | android.notification.sound | Not applicable | . | category | aps.category, so an app can register actionable categories | In message.data | In the payload | . | data and the substratal block | Top-level keys beside aps | message.data, with substratal as a JSON string | In the payload | . Web Push payloads are encrypted for the subscription’s keys (RFC 8291, aes128gcm), and every request is signed with the Application’s VAPID key (RFC 8292). APNs requests use token-based authentication with the Application’s key, and FCM requests use OAuth 2.0 access tokens minted from its service account. The platform caches and refreshes each of these, so an Application only supplies the long-lived credential. Keep sensitive content out of title, body, and data. Apple, Google, and the browser vendors’ push services carry the payload, and a lock screen shows the title and body to anyone holding the phone. For anything private, send a generic title, put an id in data, and let the app fetch the details once it’s open and authenticated. The payload is also what the Compliance page counts these providers as sub-processors for.

297.title: Delivery
297.content: . | Latency target: p95 under 10 seconds from the committing write to the first provider attempt, the same as webhooks. Deliveries are written in the same transaction as the notification, so a committed send can never lose its push. | Retries: a provider 429, a 5xx, or a timeout (5 seconds) is retried at +30 seconds, +2 minutes, and +10 minutes, for 4 attempts in total, within ttl_seconds. Then that delivery is failed. A provider’s Retry-After is honored when it’s longer. | A token the provider reports as gone deactivates the device (inactive_reason: unregistered) and fires device.deactivated. That’s APNs 410 Unregistered or 400 BadDeviceToken/DeviceTokenNotForTopic, FCM 404 UNREGISTERED or a 400 INVALID_ARGUMENT naming the token, and Web Push 404/410. Nothing is retried for that device. | A credential the provider rejects marks it failed, as described under Push credentials. Every pending delivery that depends on it is skipped. | No ordering guarantee, and a provider may deliver late or not at all. Clients should treat a push as a prompt to refresh from the API, not as the source of truth. collapse_key is the tool for “show only the latest”. | No delivery receipts. sent means the provider accepted the push. Whether the User saw it isn’t knowable from the provider, and the inbox’s read state is the only “seen” signal. | .

298.title: Sessions and device lifecycle
298.content: A device a User registers with their own token is tied to the session that registered it (session_id), so signing out stops its pushes: . | Event | Effect on devices | . | Logout, or revoking that session | Devices registered under that session become inactive (session_revoked). Logout from every session deactivates all of them. | . | Password reset, refresh-token reuse, or MFA reset (each revokes sessions) | The same, after the security.* alert is raised. | . | The User is suspended or soft-deleted, or a test-mode User expires | Every device they hold becomes inactive (user_suspended, user_deleted, or test_user_expired), including devices an app key registered. | . | The User signs in again on the same install | The client re-registers its token, which reactivates the device under the new session. | . | An app-key registration (session_id: null) | Not affected by logout, because the platform can’t see the app’s own sessions. The Application’s backend should DELETE the device when its user signs out. | . | No re-registration for 270 days | inactive (stale). Providers expire tokens from installs that are never opened, so a client should re-register on launch, at most once a day. | . | The Application’s web_push credential is deleted | Its web_push devices become inactive (credential_removed). | . | The User loses access to the Application | Devices stay active, but sends to the User are rejected (403 entitlement_required) until access returns. | . An inactive device is deleted 30 days after it was deactivated, unless it’s re-registered first.

299.title: Test mode
299.content: A test-mode key registers test-mode devices and sends test-mode notifications. Test-mode notifications reach only test-mode devices, and live notifications never reach a test-mode device, the same isolation as every other record (see API Keys → Test vs. live). Pushes are real: a test-mode delivery goes through the actual provider, using the Application’s shared credentials. Point test-mode devices at development builds (environment: sandbox on APNs) so test traffic never reaches a production install.

300.title: Webhook events
300.content: Five events tell an Application’s backend about its devices, credentials, and failed pushes. They’re delivered to the Application’s webhook subscriptions like any other event, never include a token or secret, and are scoped to their application_id: . | Event | Fires when | data | . | device.registered | A Device is created, or an inactive one is reactivated. | device | . | device.deactivated | A Device becomes inactive. | device (with inactive_reason) | . | device.deleted | A Device is deleted, by DELETE, by a registration of its token for another User, or 30 days after deactivation. | device (last state) | . | notification.push_failed | One of the Application’s own notifications ends with push.status failed, or skipped for no_devices, no_credentials, or credential_failed. Not for push_disabled or push_not_requested, which are choices rather than failures, and never for a platform alert. | notification_id, user_id, category, push | . | push_credential.failed | A credential becomes failed. | provider, failure_reason | . notification.push_failed is the hook for falling back to another channel, such as email from your own backend, when a push can’t go out.

301.title: Errors specific to this resource
301.content: | Code | Status | When | . | push_credential_not_found | 404 | {provider} isn’t configured for the Application, or isn’t one of apns, fcm, web_push. | . | push_credential_exists | 409 | POST for a provider the Application already has. | . | invalid_push_credential | 422 | Key material that doesn’t parse, or a service account missing a required field. | . | push_not_configured | 409 | A device test for a provider the Application has no credential for. | . | device_not_found | 404 | {deviceId} doesn’t resolve, isn’t the User’s, or (for an app key) belongs to another Application. | . | invalid_device_token | 422 | A token or subscription in the wrong format for its provider, or a web_push endpoint that isn’t a public https URL. | . | notification_not_found | 404 | {notificationId} doesn’t resolve or isn’t visible to the caller. | . | reserved_category | 422 | An Application’s send uses a security., account., or billing. category. | . | notification_too_large | 422 | The push payload would exceed 4 KB. details.bytes and details.max say by how much. | . | entitlement_required | 403 | The recipient (or the User registering a device) doesn’t have active access to the Application. | . | user_token_required | 400 | An API Key tried to create, change, or remove a push credential, or used me. | . | read_only_field | 422 | A PATCH touched a read-only field, such as a device’s provider or a credential’s application_id. | . | invalid_status_transition | 409 | A credential PATCH status other than failed → active. | . | rate_limited | 429 | Over the per-sender or per-recipient limit. details.scope is sender or recipient. | .

302.title: Orders & Audit
302.content: . | Order . | Billing system of record | . | Audit Event . | Example | Action catalog | What triggers an Audit Event | . | .

303.title: Order
303.content: order_id is an opaque, developer-supplied reference (no entity, table, or endpoint), following from the billing system of record. billing.manage and billing.refund apply to the one billing relationship Substratal actually has, the Free/Standard subscription. billing.manage lets support view any User’s or Organization’s subscription, list them all (GET /subscriptions), and open a billing portal. billing.refund is reserved for Stripe credits and refunds, which are done in the Stripe dashboard today, so it has no endpoint yet. An Order isn’t an entity in this API. There’s no orders table, no ord_ resource, and no Orders endpoint. The commerce record an Entitlement traces back to lives in the developer’s own billing system (see Billing system of record below). What this API stores is a reference to it: . | Field (on Entitlement) | Type | Notes | . | order_id | string, nullable, ≤ 255 characters | Opaque. Typically the developer’s own Stripe subscription id (sub_…), invoice id, or internal order number. It isn’t validated beyond its length, never dereferenced, and never used to drive state on its own. It’s settable once, so it stays a stable reconciliation key, and it’s filterable on GET /entitlements?order_id=…. | . Its one behavioral effect: an Entitlement with order_id set can’t be hard-deleted (entitlement_order_linked), because it represents a real financial event rather than a mistake. When the developer’s billing changes, for example a refund or a lapsed subscription, the developer’s backend calls this API to change the Entitlement: PATCH /entitlements/{id} with status: revoked, or by setting ends_at so it lapses on schedule, using an app-scoped API Key. This API never learns about the payment itself. See Workflows → Purchase → access. Billing system of record . Each Application’s developer owns the billing relationship with that Application’s end users, and calls Entitlements to reflect the outcome. Order/order_id is reference metadata the developer supplies for their own reconciliation, never a record that a Substratal-run billing system pushes webhooks about. Today Substratal is the developer of every Application in the catalog, so it bills those Applications’ users itself, through one subscription for the whole catalog: Free and Standard. See Pricing. That’s the only payment flow that runs through Substratal Apps. Substratal Apps is not a payment processor or marketplace billing engine for anyone else’s Application, including after the marketplace phase ships. When the marketplace ships, it makes third-party Applications discoverable, each with its developer’s own pricing and billing, entirely outside this API. It is not a checkout that Substratal runs. How a Standard subscription turns into access is in Entitlements → Platform-managed Entitlements: the platform grants and ends free and subscription Entitlements, and Applications see them like any other.

304.title: Audit Event
304.content: An immutable record of who changed what access, when. Never edited or deleted through the API, including after the record it describes is itself deleted. Only two scheduled jobs touch an event after it’s written, and both only reduce it to its shape: archival at the end of the hot window, and the erasure cascade’s redaction of before/after for a deleted User (see Non-Functional Requirements → Audit). | Field | Type | Notes | . | id | string | evt_ prefix. | . | action | string | See Action catalog below. | . | actor | object | Who made the change: { "type": "user" \| "api_key" \| "system", "id": "usr_…" \| "key_…" \| "system" }. A change made by a User through an MCP or agent session that used their own token is type: user; the audit log doesn’t distinguish which client a User’s token was used from. A change made by an API Key is type: api_key, with the key’s id. System-initiated changes, such as a trial expiring, an erasure cascade, or a Stripe sync, are type: system, id: "system". | . | target | object | What changed: { "type": "user" \| "entitlement" \| "role" \| "role_assignment" \| "application" \| "organization" \| "subscription" \| "tenant" \| "tier_change_request" \| "api_key" \| "webhook" \| "push_credential" \| "device", "id": "…" }. id is the target’s own id, with one exception: a Role assignment has no id of its own, so for role_assignment it’s the role_id, and the User is in target_user_id. | . | target_user_id | string, nullable | Whose access or data changed, when there is such a User. It’s null for events with no user subject, such as application.updated, api_key.created, or an Organization’s subscription.status_changed. For an org-wide Entitlement change it’s also null. The per-member effect shows up as access.* webhooks, not as one Audit Event per member. | . | application_id, organization_id, tenant_id | string, nullable | Scope, where relevant. tenant_id is the Tenant the change belongs to: denormalized from the Application when there is one, set directly for tenant.* events, and null for platform-level events with neither (for example user.created). | . | before / after | object, nullable | A snapshot of the changed fields only, not the whole record. Secrets and hashes never appear, even as before/after values. | . | request_id | string, nullable | The X-Request-Id of the API call that caused it, or null for system events. It joins audit to request logs. | . | timestamp | timestamp | The commit time of the change. | . Example . { "id": "evt_01JAG7X3P8QY110M9N807P6Q5R", "action": "entitlement.disabled", "actor": { "type": "user", "id": "usr_01JAG9STAFF000000000000000" }, "target": { "type": "entitlement", "id": "ent_01JAG9F4Q1W2E3R4T5Y6V7J809" }, "target_user_id": "usr_01JAG3Z9X8QS3F6K2M4N5P6R7S", "application_id": "app_invoicer", "organization_id": null, "tenant_id": "tnt_01JAG1SYSTEM00000000000000", "before": { "status": "active" }, "after": { "status": "disabled", "disabled_reason": "billing_dispute" }, "request_id": "req_7c1e9a2f4b", "timestamp": "2026-09-30T16:22:41Z" } . Action catalog . Every value action can take. It’s mirrored exactly by the AuditAction enum in openapi.yaml, and by the check constraint on audit_events.action (see Database Schema). Entries marked admin-only never fire for a self-service change. See What triggers an Audit Event below. | Action | Fires when | target.type | . | user.created | POST /users, POST /auth/signup, or an invite via org membership | user | . | user.updated | users.manage activates an invited User without a password (PATCH status: active), or changes a test-mode User’s expires_at. Suspension, reactivation, restore, email, and deletion each have their own action — admin-only | user | . | user.email_changed | An email change completes (self, after verification; or admin, immediately) | user | . | user.suspended | POST /users/{id}/suspend, or PATCH status: suspended — admin-only | user | . | user.reactivated | PATCH status: active on a suspended User, or on a soft-deleted one (a restore) — admin-only | user | . | user.deleted | DELETE /users/{id}, or the soft-delete step of an erasure request | user | . | user.expired | A test-mode User’s expires_at passes; written by the expiry sweep (actor system). See Auth → Test-mode Users → Lifetime | user | . | user.erasure_requested | POST /users/{id}/erasure-requests | user | . | user.erasure_cancelled | DELETE /users/{id}/erasure-requests/current — admin-only | user | . | user.erased | The hard-delete cascade completes (actor system) | user | . | user.password_changed | POST /users/{id}/password | user | . | user.password_reset | POST /auth/password/reset | user | . | user.mfa_enabled / user.mfa_disabled | TOTP confirmed / disabled by the user | user | . | user.mfa_reset | DELETE /users/{id}/mfa/totp — admin-only | user | . | user.sessions_revoked | POST /users/{id}/sessions/revoke-all, by the User or a users.manage caller; the count and keep_current are in after | user | . | entitlement.granted | An Entitlement is created, or returns to active. Platform-managed free and subscription rows are granted with actor system | entitlement | . | entitlement.disabled | status set to disabled | entitlement | . | entitlement.revoked | status set to revoked | entitlement | . | entitlement.expired | Automatic transition to expired (actor system) | entitlement | . | entitlement.updated | ends_at, source, or order_id changes without a status change | entitlement | . | entitlement.member_scope_changed | An org grant’s member_scope/member_overrides changes — see Entitlements → Org-wide entitlements | entitlement | . | entitlement.deleted | DELETE /entitlements/{id} (error correction) | entitlement | . | role.created / role.updated / role.deleted | Role definition changes, including Roles seeded or removed via an Application’s available_app_roles | role | . | role.assigned / role.removed | POST/DELETE /users/{id}/roles/{roleId} (only when something actually changed) | role_assignment | . | profile.updated | An admin changes another user’s Profile or AppProfile — admin-only | user | . | settings.updated | An admin changes another user’s Settings or AppSettings — admin-only | user | . | application.created | POST /applications | application | . | application.updated | PATCH /applications/{id} (configuration fields) | application | . | application.review_status_changed | A reviewer approves, rejects, suspends, or reinstates; or a rejected app is resubmitted — see Applications → The review lifecycle | application | . | organization.created / organization.updated | POST/PATCH /organizations… | organization | . | organization.member_invited | A pending membership is created by email; the person hasn’t accepted yet | organization | . | organization.member_added / organization.member_removed | A membership becomes active (accepted, or added directly by organizations.manage), or is removed, including leaving and declining | organization | . | organization.member_role_changed | PATCH /organizations/{id}/members/{userId} | organization | . | subscription.created | The first Checkout for a User or Organization creates its Subscription (status: incomplete) | subscription | . | subscription.status_changed | status changes via a Stripe sync (actor system) | subscription | . | subscription.members_changed | An org admin changes which members an Organization’s subscription covers (PATCH /organizations/{id}/subscription) | subscription | . | tenant.tier_change_requested | POST /tenants/{id}/tier-change-requests — the request itself, not yet the migration | tier_change_request | . | tenant.tier_change_request_updated | PATCH on a tier-change request (scheduled, started, cancelled) | tier_change_request | . | tenant.tier_changed | A tier-change request reaches completed: tier/region change and status returns to active — see Tenancy → How a tier change happens today | tenant | . | api_key.created / api_key.updated / api_key.rotated / api_key.revoked | API Key lifecycle | api_key | . | api_key.restrict_destructive_disabled | restrict_destructive explicitly set to false on an intended_use: "agent" key (written in addition to api_key.created/updated) — see API Keys → Agent keys | api_key | . | webhook.created / webhook.updated / webhook.deleted / webhook.secret_rotated | Webhook subscription lifecycle | webhook | . | push_credential.created / push_credential.updated / push_credential.deleted | An Application’s push credential is configured, changed, or removed. The platform marking one failed (or a change returning it to active) is push_credential.updated with actor system. Key material never appears in before/after | push_credential | . | device.deleted | users.manage deletes another User’s Device — admin-only | device | . | organization.scim_token_created / organization.scim_token_revoked | An Organization’s SCIM token is created (or rotated), or revoked | organization | . | audit.exported | An Audit Event export is written; actor is whoever requested it, with the filters, format, and row count in after | audit_export | . This list is the authoritative source for action values. If an endpoint’s page describes a write that isn’t represented here, that’s a spec bug; file it the same way as any other inconsistency. What triggers an Audit Event . Every write to an Entitlement, every Role definition or assignment change, every change to a credential (API Key, webhook secret, push credential, password, MFA), every Application, Organization, and Tenant change, and every admin-initiated (not self-service) change to a user’s Profile or Settings. Self-service changes a user makes to their own Profile/Settings aren’t audited at this level of detail. That’s ordinary account activity, not an access-control event. Not Audit Events: logins, failed logins, token refreshes, reads, a User registering their own device, and sending a notification (the Notification row records its own sender). Those go to the security log (structured application logs with X-Request-Id, retained 1 year in CloudWatch Logs; see Non-Functional Requirements → Security logging). The Audit log records changes to state, and the security log records access attempts. See Non-Functional Requirements → Audit.

306.title: Organizations
306.content: Team management, and the Organization’s own Standard subscription. Part of Phase 2, not the MVP. See Domain Model → Organization. | Endpoints | The Organization object | GET /organizations | POST /organizations | GET /organizations/{id} | PATCH /organizations/{id} | GET /organizations/{id}/members | POST /organizations/{id}/members | POST /organizations/{id}/members/me/accept | PATCH /organizations/{id}/members/{userId} | DELETE /organizations/{id}/members/{userId} | GET /organizations/{id}/entitlements | POST /organizations/{id}/entitlements | Delegated admin | Errors specific to this resource | .

307.title: Endpoints
307.content: | Method | Path | Requires | Purpose | . | GET | /organizations | any User | Your own Organizations; everything with organizations.manage. | . | POST | /organizations | any active User | Create an Organization; the caller becomes its first org_admin. | . | GET | /organizations/{id} | active member, or organizations.manage | Fetch one. | . | PATCH | /organizations/{id} | org admin (name), organizations.manage (name, status) | Rename, or suspend/reactivate. | . | GET | /organizations/{id}/members | active member, or organizations.manage | List members. | . | POST | /organizations/{id}/members | org admin (by email), or organizations.manage (by email or user_id) | Invite a member. | . | POST | /organizations/{id}/members/me/accept | the invited User | Accept a pending membership. | . | PATCH | /organizations/{id}/members/{userId} | org admin, or organizations.manage | Change a member’s role. | . | DELETE | /organizations/{id}/members/{userId} | org admin, organizations.manage, or the member themselves (me) | Remove a member, withdraw an invitation, leave, or decline. | . | GET | /organizations/{id}/entitlements | active member, or organizations.manage | List org-wide (“seat”) grants. | . | POST | /organizations/{id}/entitlements | entitlements.manage (platform, or the Application’s own confined key), or the Application’s owner | Grant an app to the whole Organization. | . | POST / GET / DELETE | /organizations/{id}/scim-token | org admin, or organizations.manage | Set up, show, or turn off SCIM provisioning. | .

309.title: GET /organizations
309.content: // Response — 200, non-admin caller (scoped to their own memberships) { "data": [ { "id": "org_01JAFZ8Y7X6W5V4V3T2S1R0Q9P", "name": "Acme Co.", "status": "active", "member_count": 42, "my_role": "org_admin", "my_membership_status": "active", "created_at": "2026-10-04T09:00:00Z" }, { "id": "org_01JAGR5S6T7V8W9X0Y1Z2A3B4C", "name": "Globex Design Team", "my_role": "member", "my_membership_status": "pending" } ], "page": { "next_cursor": null, "has_more": false } } . A non-admin caller sees every Organization they hold an OrganizationMembership in. A User can belong to more than one. my_role is that caller’s standing in each, and my_membership_status is active or pending. A pending row is an invitation waiting for the caller to accept, and shows only id, name, my_role, and my_membership_status. member_count counts active members only. A organizations.manage holder sees every Organization (with no my_role) and can filter with ?status= and ?q= (a name prefix).

310.title: POST /organizations
310.content: Self-service creation (any active User, rate-limited) is what makes team end users from Phase 2 workable, rather than a Substratal staff member creating every team. The guard that makes it safe: an org admin can never create an org-wide grant for their own Organization. Only whoever controls the Application can. Without that rule, anyone could create an Organization and grant themselves free access to any app. // Request { "name": "Acme Co." } . // Response — 201 { "id": "org_01JAFZ8Y7X6W5V4V3T2S1R0Q9P", "name": "Acme Co.", "status": "active", "member_count": 1, "created_by": "usr_01JAG3Z9X8QS3F6K2M4N5P6R7S", "test_mode": false, "created_at": "2026-10-04T09:00:00Z", "updated_at": "2026-10-04T09:00:00Z" } . Any active User may create one, with a limit of 10 per User per day (429). The caller becomes the first member, with role: org_admin, in the same transaction. A name is 1–100 characters and doesn’t have to be unique. Must be called with a User token, not an API Key (400 user_token_required). Writes organization.created.

311.title: GET /organizations/{id}
311.content: Returns the Organization object. Active members and organizations.manage only; anyone else, including someone with only a pending invitation, gets 404 organization_not_found.

312.title: PATCH /organizations/{id}
312.content: // Request — rename (org admin) { "name": "Acme Corporation" } . // Request — suspend (platform only) { "status": "suspended", "reason": "ToS investigation SUP-5120" } . // Response — 200, the full updated Organization (here, after the suspend) { "id": "org_01JAFZ8Y7X6W5V4V3T2S1R0Q9P", "name": "Acme Co.", "status": "suspended", "member_count": 42, "created_by": "usr_01JAG3Z9X8QS3F6K2M4N5P6R7S", "test_mode": false, "created_at": "2026-10-04T09:00:00Z", "updated_at": "2026-10-06T10:00:00Z" } . | An org admin may change name. Only organizations.manage can change status (403 forbidden otherwise), and reason is recorded on the Audit Event. | What suspension does: the Organization’s own admin actions freeze. Every member, entitlement, and SSO write under it returns 403 organization_suspended, and no new members can join. | What it doesn’t do: it doesn’t touch existing org-wide Entitlements or members’ access, the same non-cascading choice made for a suspended Application. A platform admin who actually wants to cut access disables or revokes the org’s grants explicitly. Destructive. | Writes organization.updated. | .

313.title: GET /organizations/{id}/members
313.content: // Response — 200 { "data": [ { "user_id": "usr_01JAG3Z9X8QS3F6K2M4N5P6R7S", "email": "jordan@example.com", "display_name": "Jordan Alvarez", "membership_status": "active", "role": "org_admin", "invited_at": "2026-10-04T09:00:00Z", "joined_at": "2026-10-04T09:05:00Z" }, { "user_id": "usr_01JAGK718M9N0P1Q2R3S4T5V6V", "email": "sam@acme.example", "display_name": null, "membership_status": "pending", "role": "member", "invited_at": "2026-10-05T08:00:00Z", "joined_at": null } ], "page": { "next_cursor": null, "has_more": false } } . Active members and organizations.manage. Filters: ?role=org_admin|member, ?membership_status=pending|active, and ?q= (a prefix of email or name). The member object deliberately says nothing about the person’s account: membership_status is the membership’s own state, and display_name is null until the membership is active. An org admin can’t use this list to learn whether an email had an account before they invited it, or what that account’s name is.

314.title: POST /organizations/{id}/members
314.content: // Request — an org admin inviting by email { "email": "sam@acme.example", "role": "member" } . // Request — organizations.manage adding a known User directly { "user_id": "usr_01JAG3Z9X8QS3F6K2M4N5P6R7S", "role": "member" } . // Response — 201 (the email invite) { "user_id": "usr_01JAGK718M9N0P1Q2R3S4T5V6V", "email": "sam@acme.example", "display_name": null, "membership_status": "pending", "role": "member", "invited_at": "2026-10-05T08:00:00Z", "joined_at": null } . | Exactly one of user_id or email is required. role defaults to member. | By email (org admins and organizations.manage): creates a pending membership and emails the address an invitation naming the Organization. If no live User has that email, an invited User is created first, and the email is the account invitation (see Auth → Invitations). This is the one way a non-platform caller can cause a User to be created. The response is the same shape either way, membership_status: "pending" and display_name: null, so inviting an address never reveals whether it already had an account. Because any User can create an Organization, anything else would let anyone test arbitrary emails for accounts. | By user_id (organizations.manage only, 403 forbidden otherwise): the membership is active immediately. Ids aren’t something an org admin can look up, and accepting on someone’s behalf is a platform action. | A pending membership grants nothing: no org-wide grant reaches the person, they’re not covered by the Organization’s subscription, and they can’t see the Organization. It becomes active when they accept, with POST …/members/me/accept if they already have an account, or by accepting the account invitation if they don’t. An unaccepted invitation never expires on its own; an org admin can withdraw it with DELETE. | Writes organization.member_invited. organization.member_added (audit and webhook) and any access.granted events fire later, on acceptance. If the address already belongs to an active User, they also get an account.organization_invitation platform alert. The caller can’t tell, so it reveals nothing the response doesn’t. | When the membership becomes active, every all_members/denylist org grant reaches the new member, including the Organization’s subscription grants, and they count toward its billed quantity from the next daily sync. | .

315.title: POST /organizations/{id}/members/me/accept
315.content: // Request {} . // Response — 200, the member object, now active { "user_id": "usr_01JAGK718M9N0P1Q2R3S4T5V6V", "email": "sam@acme.example", "display_name": "Sam Rivera", "membership_status": "active", "role": "member", "invited_at": "2026-10-05T08:00:00Z", "joined_at": "2026-10-05T08:30:00Z" } . Called with the invited User’s own token (400 user_token_required for an API Key). 404 member_not_found if the caller has no pending membership in this Organization; accepting an already-active membership returns 200 with no change. On acceptance the new member falls under every all_members/denylist org grant, access.granted fires for each Application they newly gain, and organization.member_added is written and emitted. To decline instead, the User calls DELETE /organizations/{id}/members/me.

316.title: PATCH /organizations/{id}/members/{userId}
316.content: // Request { "role": "org_admin" } . // Response — 200, the member object { "user_id": "usr_01JAGK718M9N0P1Q2R3S4T5V6V", "email": "sam@acme.example", "display_name": "Sam Rivera", "membership_status": "active", "role": "org_admin", "invited_at": "2026-10-05T08:00:00Z", "joined_at": "2026-10-05T08:30:00Z" } . Demoting the Organization’s last active org_admin returns 409 last_org_admin, because an Organization always has at least one. A pending member’s role can be changed too; it takes effect when they accept. Writes organization.member_role_changed.

317.title: DELETE /organizations/{id}/members/{userId}
317.content: // Response — 204 . | An org admin or organizations.manage can remove anyone, including withdrawing a pending invitation. Any member can remove themselves (/members/me), which for a pending membership means declining it. Removing a pending membership fires no access.* events and writes organization.member_removed only to the audit log. | Removing the last org_admin returns 409 last_org_admin. Promote someone else first. | The removed User loses every org-wide (source: org_seat) access path through this Organization. access.revoked fires for each Application where that was their only active path, so a personal Entitlement held some other way is untouched. Their user id is also removed from member_overrides on this Organization’s grants, so re-adding them later starts clean. | App Role assignments aren’t touched. Roles belong to the User, not the Organization. If the user has no other access path, those Roles simply grant nothing until they do (see Access Control). | Writes organization.member_removed, and emits the organization.member_removed webhook. Destructive. | .

318.title: GET /organizations/{id}/entitlements
318.content: // Response — 200 { "data": [ { "id": "ent_01JAGB2C3D4E5F6G7H8J9K011M", "user_id": null, "organization_id": "org_01JAFZ8Y7X6W5V4V3T2S1R0Q9P", "application_id": "app_invoicer", "status": "active", "source": "org_seat", "order_id": "sub_1QaB2cD3eF4gH5iJ", "starts_at": "2026-10-04T09:10:00Z", "ends_at": null, "member_scope": "denylist", "member_overrides": ["usr_01JAG3Z9X8QS3F6K2M4N5P6R7S"], "included_member_count": 41 } ], "page": { "next_cursor": null, "has_more": false } } . included_member_count is computed: how many active members this grant reaches (excluded members don’t count) after member_scope. Same filters as GET /entitlements.

319.title: POST /organizations/{id}/entitlements
319.content: // Request { "application_id": "app_invoicer", "order_id": "sub_1QaB2cD3eF4gH5iJ", "member_scope": "denylist", "member_overrides": ["usr_01JAG3Z9X8QS3F6K2M4N5P6R7S"] } . // Response — 201 { "id": "ent_01JAGB2C3D4E5F6G7H8J9K011M", "user_id": null, "organization_id": "org_01JAFZ8Y7X6W5V4V3T2S1R0Q9P", "application_id": "app_invoicer", "status": "active", "source": "org_seat", "order_id": "sub_1QaB2cD3eF4gH5iJ", "starts_at": "2026-10-05T12:00:00Z", "ends_at": null, "member_scope": "denylist", "member_overrides": ["usr_01JAG3Z9X8QS3F6K2M4N5P6R7S"], "included_member_count": 41 } . | Requires Idempotency-Key. source is always org_seat and isn’t accepted in the request. | order_id, starts_at, and ends_at follow the same rules as a personal grant. member_scope defaults to all_members. member_overrides must list active members only. | Who: whoever controls access to the Application, never the Organization itself. That means platform entitlements.manage, the Application’s own key with app-confined entitlements.manage (the normal path: the developer’s backend reflecting a team purchase in their own billing), or the Application’s owner. An org admin can’t create a grant for their own Organization. Organizations are self-service (POST /organizations), so allowing it would let anyone create an Organization and grant themselves free access to any app. 403 forbidden otherwise. | One live org grant per (Organization, app): 409 entitlement_already_exists if an active/disabled one exists. | Writes entitlement.granted. Emits entitlement.granted, and access.granted per newly included member. | Change the grant afterwards with PATCH /entitlements/{id} (status, term, member_scope). | . effective_permissions for an included member still resolves their own app-scoped Role on top. The org grant only answers the on/off question, same as a personal one would.

320.title: Delegated admin
320.content: An org admin is simply a User whose active OrganizationMembership has role: org_admin for that specific Organization (a pending invitation as org_admin confers nothing until accepted). It’s not a third Role scope alongside platform and application_id. This standing lets them manage their own Organization’s members, and decide who within the Organization an existing org-wide grant reaches (member_scope/member_overrides) and whether it’s switched on (active ⇄ disabled), without a platform-wide admin Role. They can’t create, revoke, re-term, or delete an org grant. Those belong to whoever controls access to the Application (see POST …/entitlements). It says nothing about their standing in any other Organization, the same independence AppRole already has across Applications. It’s unrelated to infrastructure-level admin (tenants.manage), which an org admin never holds. If the Organization owns an Application, its org admins are that Application’s owners (see Applications).

321.title: Errors specific to this resource
321.content: | Code | Status | When | . | organization_not_found | 404 | {id} doesn’t resolve, or the caller isn’t a member. | . | organization_suspended | 403 | Any org-admin write on a suspended Organization, and accepting an invitation to one. | . | forbidden | 403 | An org admin adding by user_id, or an org admin creating an org-wide grant. | . | user_not_found | 404 | organizations.manage added a user_id that doesn’t resolve. | . | already_member | 409 | Inviting or adding a user who’s already a member, pending or active. | . | member_not_found | 404 | {userId} isn’t a member. | . | last_org_admin | 409 | Removing or demoting the last org_admin. | . | member_override_not_a_member | 422 | A member_overrides id isn’t an active member. | . | entitlement_already_exists | 409 | A live org grant for this app already exists. | .

322.title: Pricing
322.content: Two subscription tiers, Free and Standard. The customer is the person using Substratal’s apps and services: an individual who subscribes for themselves, or an Organization that subscribes for its members. | The tiers . | Business and Enterprise | . | Who pays | What a “user” means for an Organization | How access follows the tier | When a subscription lapses | Stripe catalog | Why two tiers | How the subscription is charged | Keeping these numbers honest | .

323.title: The tiers
323.content: For most people, Free or Standard is all they’ll ever need. |   | Free | Standard | . | Price | $0 | $6 per user per month | . | What it includes | Access to the Applications, features, and services Substratal designates as free. | Access to download and use every Application and service Substratal Apps offers, including everything in Free. | . | Who can subscribe | Every User, automatically, with no card required. | A User for themselves, or an Organization for its members. | . | Billing | None. | Monthly, USD, tax-exclusive, through Stripe Billing. | . Free and Standard are the only tiers available today. Business and Enterprise . Beyond Standard there will be business and enterprise pricing, tailored to an Organization’s specific needs, tenancy, and the geographic location of its data. It isn’t offered yet and has no published price. The infrastructure it will be built on is already specified: the isolated and dedicated_region Tenant tiers and the support-run tier-change process. Until business pricing ships, everything runs on the shared tier.

324.title: Who pays
324.content: Substratal builds every Application in the catalog today (see Home), so Substratal bills the people who use those Applications directly, through this subscription. Nobody pays per Application. A Standard subscription covers the whole catalog. There are two ways to be covered by Standard: . | Individual subscription. A User subscribes for themselves: one user, $6 a month. | Organization subscription. An Organization subscribes for its members and pays $6 a month for each covered member (see What a “user” means for an Organization). An org admin chooses which members are covered, with the same all_members / allowlist / denylist choice that org-wide Entitlements already use. | . A User covered either way has Standard access. Someone covered by an Organization can still subscribe individually. Both subscriptions are billed, and the User’s plan_sources lists both so a client can suggest cancelling one; nothing is refunded automatically. When a third-party marketplace ships, its Applications will carry their own developers’ pricing and billing. This subscription covers Substratal’s own catalog only (see Orders & Audit → Billing system of record).

325.title: What a “user” means for an Organization
325.content: An Organization is billed for each covered member: a distinct, non-test-mode User who is an active member of the Organization and is included by its subscription’s member selection. Suspended and deleted Users don’t count, and neither do pending invitations. A User who belongs to several Organizations that each subscribe is counted by each of them. The count is provisioned, not activity-based. It counts who is covered, not who signed in this month, so an Organization can predict and budget against it. The count syncs to Stripe once a day with no mid-period proration. Each invoice charges for the count on the day before it’s issued. Real-time sync with prorations was considered and not chosen: it’s more accurate, but noisier for customers and means more Stripe API calls. A live subscription never counts test-mode Users, so integration tests can’t consume paid seats. A test-mode subscription runs in Stripe test mode and counts only test-mode members whose expires_at hasn’t passed. Test-mode Users last 24 hours by default and never more than 30 days, so test mode can’t stand in for a free production tier.

326.title: How access follows the tier
326.content: Every Application is designated either free or standard. | A free Application is available to every active User. | A standard Application is available to every User covered by Standard, through their own subscription or an Organization’s. | . Access is still enforced through Entitlements and the access-control algorithm, exactly as for any other grant. The platform keeps them in step with each Application’s tier and each subscription (see Platform-managed Entitlements): . | Every User gets a free Entitlement to each free Application at signup. | A subscription that covers someone gives them a subscription Entitlement to each standard Application: a personal one for an individual subscription, or one org-wide grant per Application for an Organization’s. | When an Application changes tier, or a new one is published, the platform grants or ends these Entitlements to match. An hourly job repairs anything that drifted. | . An admin can still disable, and later re-enable, one person’s access to one Application, whatever their tier. Applications hear about every change through the usual access.granted / access.revoked webhooks.

327.title: When a subscription lapses
327.content: | Situation | What happens | . | Payment fails (past_due) | Nothing changes. Stripe retries (Smart Retries, about 3 weeks) and emails the customer. | . | Subscription ends (canceled, unpaid, incomplete_expired, paused) | Standard access ends at the end of the paid period. The User, or every member the Organization covered, drops to Free. | . | A member leaves an Organization, or the org admin stops covering them | They lose Standard access through that Organization at once. They’re no longer counted from the next daily sync. | . | Voluntary cancellation | Cancel at period end in the Stripe Customer Portal. Standard access continues until then. | . Dropping to Free never deletes anything. Profiles, settings, and per-user data in standard Applications are kept, and come back when the User is covered by Standard again. Only access to standard Applications stops.

328.title: Stripe catalog
328.content: Free is a User with no Stripe Subscription. Upgrades go through Stripe Checkout, and payment methods, invoices, and cancellation through the Customer Portal. Billing is monthly, USD only, and tax-exclusive with Stripe Tax. The Products and Prices configured in Stripe. Lookup keys are what the code references, never Stripe price ids, so test and live mode can share code. | Product | Price lookup key | Amount | Shape | . | Substratal Standard | standard_monthly_usd | $6.00 per user | Licensed (not metered), billing_scheme: per_unit, monthly. quantity: 1 for an individual subscription. For an Organization, quantity is the covered-member count from the daily sync, at least 1. | . | Free has no Stripe Subscription, and a User or Organization has no Stripe Customer until its first Checkout. That avoids $0 subscriptions that would need cancelling and replacing on upgrade. | Monthly, USD, tax-exclusive (Stripe Tax enabled). There are no annual plans and no Standard trial: Free is the way to try Substratal’s apps, and it never needs a card. Either can be added later as Stripe configuration (a second price, or subscription_data.trial_period_days on Checkout) without an API change. | Organization quantity is written to the subscription item by a daily job (00:15 UTC) with proration_behavior: none. | Business and Enterprise prices will be created per customer when those tiers ship. | .

329.title: Why two tiers
329.content: . | Free is free, not just cheap. The first horizon in Growth trajectory is dozens of users, and the shared-tier cost of serving free Applications is near zero against the infrastructure floor that’s paid regardless. Charging for it would tax exactly the adoption the product needs most right now. | One paid price, for the whole catalog. A single per-user price is easy to understand and budget for, and works the same for one person or a whole Organization. Per-Application pricing would make every new Application a new purchasing decision. | Infrastructure choice waits for business pricing. isolated and dedicated_region tenancy carry a real, named infrastructure cost, driven by a customer’s own compliance or data-residency requirement. That’s what business and enterprise pricing is for, so neither is offered on Free or Standard. | .

330.title: How the subscription is charged
330.content: The subscription is processed through Stripe Billing. Card data never touches this API, and Stripe is PCI-DSS Level 1, which keeps PCI scope minimal (see Compliance). Stripe is one of the platform’s two sub-processors, alongside AWS (see Compliance → GDPR (and CCPA)). The implementation (object mapping, webhook event handling, the daily quantity sync) is specified in infra/README.md → Stripe Billing. It’s a build and operations concern, not part of the API Applications call.

331.title: Keeping these numbers honest
331.content: Stripe’s official MCP server is the direct way to check that the Products and Prices configured in Stripe still match this page. The two are kept in sync by hand, the same relationship Conventions → Machine-readable describes between this site’s prose and openapi.yaml. When business pricing is designed, the AWS Pricing and AWS Billing and Cost Management MCP servers are the way to ground its tenancy surcharges in live infrastructure cost rather than estimates.

346.title: The split: global vs. per-app
346.content: Identity data comes in two layers. Profile is who the user is, site-wide. AppProfile is who they are inside one specific app — data that only makes sense scoped to that product and that the global Profile shouldn’t be cluttered with. | Field | Global Profile | AppProfile (per User × Application) | . | display_name, avatar_url | ✓ | Not stored per app. display_handle (below) overrides the name for display inside the app, and the API returns effective_display_name so the app never re-implements the fallback. The avatar is always the global one. | . | display_handle | — | ✓ an app-local identity, e.g. a username meaningful only inside one product | . | contact email/phone | ✓ | — | . | custom fields | — | ✓ arbitrary JSON the owning app defines for itself | .
